content:
MASSIVE: OpenAI just claimed its new Jalapeño chips delivered 104.3x more throughput per kilowatt than NVIDIA GB300 at matched DeepSeek R1 decoding speed.

The figure comes from GB300's previous-best time-between-token speed: at 169.41 tok/s/user, Jalapeño produced 12,258 mixed tokens/s/kW versus 118 for GB300.

The tests used SemiAnalysis's public InferenceX benchmark, which measures full-request throughput, power efficiency, and latency.

- Jalapeño is rated at 700W, compared with 1,200W for GB200 and 1,400W for GB300

- OpenAI attributes the efficiency to keeping KV-cache and model state local, reducing data movement as inference switches between compute-heavy prefill and memory-bound decoding.

- OpenAI plans deployment by year-end, with Gen 2 already well underway and Gen 3 taking shape

- AI also helped move Jalapeño from initial design to tapeout in nine months, and selected AI-generated GPT-OSS kernels ran 1.5 to 1.8x faster than human-expert implementations on selected blocks.

title:
More details on OpenAI’s Jalapeño chip from SemiAnalysis:

SemiAnalysis says Jalapeño is not narrowly optimized for OpenAI models. 

It is a general-purpose inference ASIC, and in the workloads they t
content:
More details on OpenAI’s Jalapeño chip from SemiAnalysis:

SemiAnalysis says Jalapeño is not narrowly optimized for OpenAI models. 

It is a general-purpose inference ASIC, and in the workloads they tested it outperformed $NVDA, $AMD and Google accelerators on several inference efficiency metrics.

The chip was designed from scratch for LLM inference and went from initial team buildout to tape-out in roughly 16 months.

Performance:
• DeepSeek R1 exceeded 700 tokens/sec/user at concurrency 1

• Kimi K2.5 and GPT-OSS reached roughly 1,400 tokens/sec/user in selected tests

• Jalapeño achieved these results using single-token prediction, without speculative decoding or prefill/decode disaggregation

• SemiAnalysis says its output-token throughput per MW already exceeds the published July Vera Rubin results, despite Rubin using multi-token prediction

• On performance per total cost, Jalapeño and Vera Rubin are currently roughly comparable based on available results

These are still early benchmarks. 

SemiAnalysis tested 8k/1k workloads and has not yet run its more demanding AgentX benchmark, which stresses long-context, multi-turn agentic workloads. Rubin is also already beginning to ship, while Jalapeño remains at the engineering-sample stage.

Hardware:
• Built on TSMC N3P
• 700W TDP
• HBM4 with 15.4TB/s of memory bandwidth

• SemiAnalysis says that is currently the highest memory bandwidth per package among shipping/near-shipping accelerators

• A0 silicon produced the current benchmark results

• B0 is already in the fab and is expected to improve perf/W by roughly 25%

• B0 delivers 13.4 PFLOPs of MXFP4 versus 17.5 PFLOPs of dense NVFP4 for a similarly sized Rubin compute die, but at lower power

Scale:
• 128 Jalapeño ASICs per rack
• Up to 2,048 XPUs can be connected across a 16-rack scale-up domain

• A complete host + ASIC rack pair consumes roughly 160kW

• OpenAI’s next deployment target is around 100MW

OpenAI is also using Codex heavily in the chip’s development. SemiAnalysis says AI-assisted design reduced SIMD area by 8% and matrix-engine area by 10%, while Codex has been used to write and optimize kernels for new models.

Production is expected to ramp gradually through 2027, with most output currently planned for Q4 2027.

content:
Today, I’m open-sourcing /fuck-cancer, an AI skill that helps patients and caregivers navigate cancer diagnosis and treatment and advocate for themselves and their loved ones.

Here’s what patients and caregivers have told me since I shared my mom’s story:

“You have to be a huge patient advocate. Ask questions and push for answers, biopsies, and proper testing.”

“I need help navigating difficult conversations and advocating for myself.”

“The volume of doctors, documents, and insurance paperwork can quickly become overwhelming.”

I built the skill to help with these problems. It creates and updates a practical brief with five sections:

1. Patient and care-team information for easy reference during calls

2. What to do next, limited to three specific actions

3. What we know, separating confirmed facts from what remains unclear

4. Medical terms explained in plain English

5. A care log with recent updates and decisions

It builds this brief from documents, and context you provide. When research is needed, it uses trusted sources such as the National Cancer Institute and the ClinicalTrials gov API.

I use it with ChatGPT/Codex and Claude Code to prepare for conversations and research. It can save the brief locally as a Markdown file or update a shareable Google Doc so the whole family can work from the same information.

https://t.co/YUGoFbhnNc

If you find it useful, please ⭐ the repo and share it with someone going through this BS disease.

Huge upgrade for local AI: Apple introduces M6 and M5 Ultra for a "big leap in performance and AI compute."  Capable of running even quantized 70B-class models locally

The new M6 model offers (tl;dr):

- Up to 4.8x faster LLM prompt processing than M4
- 42% more memory bandwidth at 170GB/s
- 12-core CPU and GPU
- Dual 16-core Neural Engine
- Up to 32GB unified memory

The M5 Pro version goes up to 64GB RAM and 307GB/s, making it capable of running even quantized 70B-class models locally.

The catch: 32GB limits the regular M6 to smaller models. It should be excellent for 7B–14B models and usable for quantized 30B models, but serious local AI users should choose the 64GB M5 Pro. Anyways, really really cool release!!

content:
AI agents are becoming a serious engineering discipline.

But the biggest mistake is trying to learn everything at once.

A better approach?

Follow a roadmap.

This AI Agent Engineering roadmap breaks the journey into 8 practical layers:

01 — LLM Fundamentals
Understand transformers, tokenization, context windows, reasoning models and benchmarks.

02 — Context Engineering
Learn how system prompts, few-shot examples, structured context and extended thinking shape agent behavior.

03 — Memory Architecture
Build session memory, vector retrieval, persistent memory and prompt caching.

04 — Agentic Workflows
Move into ReAct patterns, MCP, multi-agent orchestration and coding agents.

05 — Tool Connectivity
Connect agents to APIs, MCP servers, browsers and computer-use tools.

06 — AI Gateways & Cost Control
Learn model routing, fallbacks, cost tracking and multi-provider setups.

07 — Guardrails & Safety
Handle prompt injection, validation, PII, jailbreaks and hallucination risks.

08 — Observability & Evaluation
Trace agent decisions, run evaluations, regression tests and detect performance drift.

The important part?

Don’t jump straight into building “autonomous agents.”

First understand the model.

Then the context.

Then memory.

Then tools.

Then orchestration.

And finally, build the systems that make agents safe, measurable and reliable.

That’s the difference between simply using AI…

…and actually understanding AI agent engineering.

Save this roadmap if you’re serious about learning agentic AI.

If you are letting AI agents write large chunks of your codebase, here is something I would recommend - decide your tradeoff per file, not as a blanket policy.

You cannot get both. Ship faster with A
content:
If you are letting AI agents write large chunks of your codebase, here is something I would recommend - decide your tradeoff per file, not as a blanket policy.

You cannot get both. Ship faster with AI-generated code, and deeply understand the codebase you are shipping. Trying to have both everywhere just means you get neither properly.

I recommend - sort modules within a codebase into two buckets before you hand anything to an agent.

Bucket one is code where being fast matters more than knowing every line. Think one-off scripts, internal tooling, throwaway prototypes. Let the agent own these fully. Do not waste your "attention" re-deriving understanding you will never need again.

Bucket two is code where a failure is expensive or hard to reverse. Think auth, payments, anything touching data integrity. For this bucket, treat the agent's output as a first draft. Read the diff line by line, trace how it touches the rest of the system, and make the agent explain its own reasoning before you merge.

If you pick one side for everything, you are smart enough to figure out what you would be losing out on. I would not repeat and restate the obvious :)

So spend the time you saved on shipping fast by reading deeply, but only where it counts. That is the whole tradeoff.

Hope this helps.

content:
I'm officially Linux pilled

Over the weekend I installed Omarchy on my old gaming computer

Since then I've absolutely fallen in love with using computers again

Rough notes on why using it is so great, and why I think you need to give it a try:

• SUPER performant. Runs incredibly well on an old Dell Alienware computer from years ago that was just sitting in my closet collecting dust

• No floating windows just makes sense. By default, all windows in Omarchy auto tile rather than float. Every time you open an app, it splits the screen further automatically. I find it impossible to go back to floating windows on Mac now. Feels archaic and sluggish to manage

• No bloatware. Windows for me has become completely unusable the last few years. Copilot, ads, and all the extras that manufacturers include with it has made it the most unpleasant experience in computers. Omarchy comes with none of that.

• Feels built for AI. Basically every harness including Codex and Grok Bot have native apps for Omarchy.

• Built for productivity. Switching workspaces and using the keyboard for basically everything just feels snappy and quick

• Makes computing fun again. Something about the whole experience is just FUN. Learning all the new key bindings, making my set up personal and my own. I got home every night this weekend just looking forward to getting back to my computer.

HIGHLY HIGHLY HIGHLY recommend trying Omarchy out for yourself.

You don't need to buy a new computer for this. It can run on really old hardware. Just grab a laptop or desktop from your closet and set it up. Ask your agent how to flash a thumb drive so you can install it.

Codex basically did the entire setup and installation for me

The learning curve is really small. As long as you have an agent up and ask it questions any time you're confused, it should be able to help you out.

And if you install tailscale and connect it to your private network, your agents can even control it from other computers.

Altho it's not necessary, I'm going to pick up a Framework laptop to use this. Need to take this on the go.

title: Pro tip if you run Codex and Claude Code at the same time. Codex writes every session to disk as a live JSONL file in ~/.codex/sessions while it works. Paste the codex:// deep link into Claude and it
content:
Pro tip if you run Codex and Claude Code at the same time. Codex writes every session to disk as a live JSONL file in ~/.codex/sessions while it works. Paste the codex:// deep link into Claude and it will find that exact thread and read everything Codex is doing in real time. Fable watching Sol. Costs you nothing, no plugin, no dashboard, no MCP server.

The UUID in the deep link is the same UUID in the rollout filename, so Claude goes straight to the file. It sees the prompts, the tool calls, the command output, the diffs, the token burn, even the sub-agents Codex spawns on its own. You get the full trace, not just the summary Codex decided to show you.

This matters because Codex telling you the tests passed is not proof the tests passed. Claude reading the actual command output in the rollout file is. One model does the work, the other one verifies it against the record, and you stop discovering the lie few commits later.

One thing to know before you try it. These files get fat fast, mine hit 30 MB on a long thread. Tell Claude to tail the last few hundred lines or filter with jq instead of reading the whole file, otherwise you torch your context window on a transcript you already lived through.

You can also just ask it what's running right now. A live Codex session holds a writer lock on its rollout, so Claude can tell you which threads are still active and which ones died. Ask it what Codex has been doing since this morning and you get a timeline back.

content:
if you're vibe coding blockchain apps make sure to care about these:

1. tell your LLM to use every single possible tool for security audits, not one, not two

and have it care about logic, math, and gas optimization

once everything is done go for testnet, fix what's broken, and then once you are ready then send your contract to audits, mentioning audit firms that you already have done preliminary audits with tools, to lower pricing, as it's gonna take them less time to fix everything due to what you polished already

2. care about your RPC subscription to be high enough for the visitors you expect, don't start with a too low RPC sub, as it's one of the most important things to make sure your app works smoothly

3. Make sure that you have your LLMs first research online documentations on how best blochain apps in your area does things

If you don't they will invent ceremonies and architectures that are utterly stupid, that will take so long to fix

Apply state-of-the art ways of doing things and don't give them too much legroom there, otherwise they'll turn things into a soup

4. Never launch any contract to the mainnet without an external audit, if you don't have the budget, enter some hackathons, put in your last money if you have to, but don't launch without audits

The risk is not worth it, even if all your LLM audits have been passing perfectly with all the security tooling

5. don't change anything in any smart contract and deploy to public, even one line after an audit is done, if you must than after adjustments contact your auditor and get them to try to look at it for free or make them agree at a very very low cost (as most are ok with this)

As long as you care about the above things, you can build anything with the right LLMs

Also avoid Claude: notoriously awful because it blocks you from doing stuff constantly while using Fable (and you wanna use the best model)

Codex asks you for a KYC for smart contract related work: if you are not comfortable giving all your info, avoid using it on smart contracts

Interestingly best model i've found on smart contract heavy work is Grok 4.6, and Kimi K3, as they don't block you for trying to make your smart contract more secure

Finally, don't be afraid of building onchain, just do your prep well by all means, and after that if something happens at least you won't blame yourself.

So many opportunities and products to build here, seize the opportunity imo..

My Codex never spoke to your Claude Code. Yet it finished a task your Claude Code had started, referencing a decision you made 20 minutes earlier that existed nowhere except in your conversation.

Here's how. ↓

Most multi-agent tools share messages: a chat channel where agents exchange a summary after a task is finished, or a relay where one agent passes the result to the next without exposing the actual process to anyone.

Tutti · VM shares something different: the complete working state. A multi-layer virtualization architecture brings your local agent, with its own configuration and subscription, into a shared cloud workspace.

There is no second copy of your work being kept in step somewhere. Your agent keeps running on your machine. You connect it to a Room once, and from then on every instruction you give it inside that Room executes locally while the whole process stays available in the Room: the ongoing conversation, the modified files, the running processes, the tasks in progress. Nothing to reconcile, nothing to wait for.

So my agent, which has never exchanged a single word with yours, can resume your exact conversation, inherit your decisions, and continue from the same point with a single @.

It goes further than a handoff. Both agents can work on the same project at the same time, and Tutti · VM resolves the conflicts in the background. Two agents editing the same page would normally mean overwritten changes and versions fighting each other. Here it just works.

You each stay in control of your own goals, permissions, and final approval. What changes is that several people and several agents share one workspace, instead of each of you running your own agent in your own corner.

Two more cases, same principle. If your Claude Code runs out mid-task, I can authorize my Codex for you: you drive it with your own context, my login never leaves my machine, and I can pull it back anytime.

And the localhost i just built runs on my machine, yet you can browse it live from yours with one link. It was never deployed anywhere.

Why does that happen?

✨ What is AI Latency?

AI
content:
You've probably noticed that some AI responses arrive almost instantly, while others take several seconds.

Why does that happen?

That's AI latency.

Let's break it down. 👇

✨ What is AI Latency?

AI latency is the time it takes for an AI system to respond to a request.

A simplified flow looks like :

User Request → Model Processing → Response

The longer this takes, the higher the latency.

  What affects AI latency?

Several things can contribute :

1. Model size : larger models generally require more computation

2. Context size : more input tokens can take longer to process

3. Output length : generating more tokens takes more time

4. Reasoning effort : deeper reasoning can increase response time

5. Tool calls : APIs, databases, or external tools add additional steps

6. Infrastructure : GPUs, servers, networking, and system load all matter

Latency isn't just "how fast is the final answer"

Developers often care about Time to First Token (TTFT). TTF is how long it takes before the model starts generating a response.

For streaming AI applications :

Request
  ↓
TTFT
  ↓
First token appears
  ↓
More tokens generated
  ↓
Final response

A system can therefore feel fast even if the complete response takes longer, as long as the first tokens appear quickly.

✨ Why does latency matter?

High latency can make an AI application feel slow and frustrating.

For production systems, developers often have to balance:

→ Quality
→ Cost
→ Speed

A more capable model isn't always the best choice if the application needs an instant response.

AI latency isn't determined by the model alone.

The entire pipeline matters from the context you send to the model, to reasoning, tool calls, infrastructure, and response generation.

That's especially important for AI applications like Cursor, Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, and Bug0, where users expect complex AI tasks to happen without waiting forever.

Thank you for reading! 🙌

if we’re going to let AI agents operate like autonomous developers, we’re going to need security tools built specifically for them

and the fact that this one is open-source makes it even more interesting

content:
Don't upgrade to the $100 Claude plan if you keep hitting token limits. Instead, use these 21 hacks to make the $20/month subscription enough:

Hack 1. Do not upload PDFs in Claude. It costs a huge amount of tokens. Paste the text into a Google Doc & download it as .md. it is not the same.

Hack 2. Figure out the solution in Chat on Fable 5 High & then move to Opus 5 on High effort to execute the task.

Hack 3. Start any new Claude chat with this prompt: “I need [task] for [goal]. I will know it worked when [target]. Ask me questions first, using the AskUserQuestion tool.”

Hack 4. When one specific thing is wrong, fix that section, not the entire thing. Prompt: "Only redo section 3. Keep everything else. Just the output."

Hack 5. Give the entire task at one go, not one problem after another in different prompts. Like: "Summarize this, list the points, suggest a headline" 

Hack 6. Stop sending follow-up prompts like "no, I meant...". Click 'Edit' on your original message to fix a specific problem.

Hack 7. Turn your repeated prompts into Claude Skills. It saves you time & tokens.

Hack 8. Use Sonnet only for grammar checks. I'd use ChatGPT, not even Sonnet. Use Fable for complex tasks. Use Opus to execute the tasks. 

Hack 9. Do not create .md files as a part of workflow. It's too much work for less outcome. Instead turn them into Claude Skills.

Hack 10. When Claude starts to hallucinate, click "edit" on an earlier message.

Hack 11. Once you send 15-20 prompts in a chat. Do not continue with that chat; instead, ask for a summary. Copy the brief. Open a fresh chat.

Hack 12. Put files in a Project. Now every chat inside that project has the same context overall.

Hack 13. Upload only the files a single task needs. Do not unnecessarily give context; it makes it less creative. 

Hack 14. One chat for one problem. It doesn't need more explanation.

Hack 15. Turn off search & connectors. Switch them on if you need them for a task.

Hack 16. Use Claude Schedule for mundane tasks over weeks. Type /schedule: "Every Monday at 7 am, create my weekly briefing."

Hack 17. This is for people who use Claude Code. Point Claude Code at the file, not the whole repo. "Build a bar chart from this CSV. Save as chart.png."

Hack 18. Go to Claude settings > Personal Preferences. Set your tone.

Hack 19. "Make it better" doesn't mean anything in Claude's language. Give more context. I speak my prompts with wispr .ai to give the full context at one go.

Hack 20. Claude uses a rolling 5-hour window. So I usually send something right when I arrive at the office and then early + late afternoon. So about 3 sessions.

Hack 21. Claude is not an all-rounder model. It can't generate good images. Use ChatGPT for image generation.

I have been using these hacks, not only to save tokens but also to get more creativity out of Claude.

I'm a psycho when it comes to using Claude (better). And I squeezed every personal tip into this one PDF. Get it here: https://t.co/KNO2y4RkYr

content:
Colby McHenry built a local knowledge graph that stops Claude Code from re-reading files it already saw.

It's called CodeGraph. Instead of grep, glob, and Read looping through your repo one file at a time, the agent asks one question and gets back the exact source, the call paths between symbols, and the blast radius of a change. No re-crawling structure it already found last turn.

→ MIT licensed, fully free
→ Local SQLite database, native Rust kernel for parsing
→ 20+ languages, from TypeScript and Python to Rust, Swift, and COBOL
→ Works with Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Gemini, Antigravity, Kiro, and GitHub Copilot
→ Auto-syncs on every file save, no manual re-indexing
→ 100% local, no API keys, nothing leaves your machine

The real numbers come from YC's own re-measured benchmark across 7 real open-source repos, Claude Opus 4.8, median of 4 runs per arm, with the CLI blocked in both arms so the control is actually a control.

The result: 88% fewer tool calls, 53% faster, 62% fewer tokens, 44% cheaper on average. On VS Code specifically, the agent went from 28 tool calls down to 2. Zero file reads across all seven repos when CodeGraph was available.

There's one honest tradeoff in the README worth knowing: CodeGraph's dense answers stay resident in context longer than a grep-and-read agent's scattered small results do, so long sessions in a small context window need to budget for that.

Still early, still improving, but the benchmark methodology here is unusually transparent about its own contamination risks.

16GB unified memory.

Then the context gets pushed to almost 50,000 tokens.

Meanwhile, the 8GB Mac is already sitting at 7.51GB used out of 8GB.

That's the part I think people still underestimate.

Local AI isn't one giant hardware market anymore.

A $4,000 RTX 5090 setup, a 96GB Strix Halo box and an old M1 MacBook aren't competing for the same job.

They're different rungs.

The mistake is buying hardware for the model you wish you needed instead of the work you actually do.

If an 8B model can handle your coding, documents, automation and daily tasks, why are you pricing a 32GB GPU?

And that's where the subscription math gets interesting.

A lot of people are still paying every month for AI without ever checking what the laptop already sitting on their desk can do.

The best local AI machine might not be the fastest one.

It might be the one you already own.

content:
CLAUDE + LOOP + GRAPH ENGINEERING: ANDREW NG'S PLAYBOOK FOR AGENTS

architecture beats model choice. every time

it starts with one loop. an agent revising its own work. everything else is that same idea, scaled up

reflect -> tools -> plan -> collaborate -> graph

> reflection - a critic checks the output against a rubric. 10-30% quality lift, day one
> tools - code, search, a database. stops hallucinating, starts checking
> planning - a plan gets written first. reroutes when a tool fails
> multi-agent - coder, reviewer, tester. different rubrics catch different errors
> graph - shared state everyone reads and writes to. the loop forgets, the graph doesn't

what it looks like on disk:

agent-system/
├── loop/
│   ├── critic.md - the rubric it checks itself against
│   └── https://t.co/mf9srjzQDj - reruns until it passes
├── tools/
│   └── tools.json - code exec, search, db query
├── plan/
│   └── plan.md - steps written before it acts
├── roles/
│   ├── coder.md
│   ├── reviewer.md
│   └── tester.md
└── graph/
    └── state.json - the memory every role reads and writes

a loop externalizes revision. a graph externalizes state. each stage fixes what broke in the one before it

Log everything."

Then the rules:

Minimum 100 trades. Max drawdown under 20%. Profit factor above 1.1. Has to beat buy and hold on that coin.

Walk away.

Come back in 2 hours.

Most results will be rubbish but it's all part of the process.

Finding good strategies means filtering out the bad one's.

My last run gave me 117% net profit, 358 trades, profit factor 1.44, 10.9% drawdown.

Put the best strategy on TradingView and run it on live data for 3 months minimum.

99% of backtests die here.

On Bybit, create an API key and secret.

Trading access only, never withdrawal access.

content:
Stop juggling AI accounts across your coding tools.

Quotio is a native macOS app for managing a local proxy for AI coding agents, built for developers using multiple AI providers and CLI tools.

It helps you centralize provider accounts, track quotas, and configure compatible agents from one place instead of switching between provider dashboards and tool configs.

Key features:

• Multi-provider accounts – connect Claude, OpenAI Codex, Qwen, Vertex AI, GitHub Copilot, and other listed providers via OAuth, API keys, or service-account JSON
• Quota visibility – view per-account quotas and use standalone mode for quick checks without running the proxy
• Agent setup – auto-detect and configure tools including Claude Code, Codex CLI, Amp CLI, OpenCode, and Factory Droid
• Live operations dashboard – monitor request traffic, token usage, success rates, and raw request/response logs
• Routing controls – choose Round Robin or Fill First failover strategies and receive alerts for low quotas, cooling periods, or service issues

It’s open-source (MIT license).

Link in the reply 👇

content:
SpaceXAI just released a new update for Grok Build.

Update to v1.0.9 

Features:
• New sessions in the interactive TUI now start in auto mode by default for fewer approval prompts.
• /feedback now supports attaching images (screenshots etc.).
• The / slash menu is now ordered by recency and groups skills below commands for easier navigation.
• /workflow now accepts --agent-budget N or an agent_budget JSON field to set child-agent limits.
• /workflow now accepts --effort LEVEL or an effort JSON field to set child reasoning effort.
• MCP servers now receive a grok-cli User-Agent header so providers can attribute traffic.
• Dashboard now lets you start new agents in Auto mode via Shift+Tab.
• Workflows now appear alongside skills in the model prompt so the agent can launch them by name.
• /edit-prompt now opens an external editor from the full TUI, not only minimal mode.
• Up arrow on an empty prompt now selects queued follow-ups first instead of opening history.
• /plugin now works as an alias for /plugins in the TUI.
• Plugin-provided agents now appear in the /agents modal and can be toggled.
• /minimal and /fullscreen now switch instantly inside the running session without restarting or losing the current turn.
• The configurable status line row now appears at the bottom of minimal mode as well as fullscreen.
• grok clone now fetches only the selected branch tip by default, with --full-history for legacy full clones.
• grok clone can now reuse a matching local checkout as a linked worktree instead of always fetching from the network.

Bug Fixes:
• Subagent tasks are more resilient to temporary rate limits and will retry instead of failing immediately.
• Narrow allow rules for Bash commands now correctly permit file writes without extra prompts.
• Rules containing markdown headings now render correctly in the prompt.
• /new and /clear now preserve the last-chosen reasoning effort instead of resetting to the model default.
• Prompt dropdowns (slash, history, file search) now have consistent left alignment with the composer.
• History now shows every command, slash command, and memory note in the order you typed them.
• Collapsed tool-call rows no longer show a vertical accent line beside the status diamond.
• Hint text above the prompt now lines up with the text you type.
• Pressing Esc while peeking at a conversation from the dashboard now closes open modals instead of leaving the view.
• /copy now preserves markdown formatting such as headings and code fences.
• Sending a new message while a shell command is running now moves the command to the background instead of cancelling it.
• grok mcp add now correctly treats bare http(s):// URLs as HTTP servers instead of stdio commands.
• Plan mode no longer incorrectly blocks subagent spawns as file edits outside plan.md.
• MCP servers that share a URL but have different names are now kept as separate entries instead of being collapsed.
• Subagents and workflow-spawned agents no longer receive the workflow tool that only top-level sessions can use.
• Memory results are now presented as historical context that should be verified against live sources before use.
• Interactive grok sessions now start in ask mode by default again instead of auto.
• Minimal mode no longer truncates subagent wake-turn replies after the first token.

Performance:
• Concurrent subagents no longer trigger rate-limit errors during bursts.
• MCP server connections no longer delay session startup when many servers are configured.

Download Grok Build: https://t.co/cB9Y5CyF8v
Update to the latest Alpha release: grok update --alpha
Update to the latest Stable release: grok update

content:
The next phase of enterprise AI will not be won by the smartest chatbot.

It will be won by the systems companies are actually willing to trust with real work.

@googlecloud just launched Gemini Enterprise for Legal.

Not simply a model for lawyers.

A governed agent platform that can review contracts, monitor regulation, research legal issues, draft documents and operate across existing legal systems while inheriting the permissions already in place.

That distinction matters.

In high stakes industries, intelligence alone is not enough.

The AI needs to know what it can access.

What it is allowed to do.

Which source it used.

Where confidentiality boundaries sit.

And when a human still needs to make the decision.

I think this is where enterprise agents become genuinely interesting.

The moat is moving from who has the cleverest model to who can safely connect intelligence to the messy systems where actual work happens.

title:
After scaling a bootstrapped SaaS from 1 to 8M$ ARR in 1 year, here are my top 10 tips to grow any SaaS.

1. Get in the mud.

If your SaaS stays inside your pitch deck, it is already dead. Five years
content:
After scaling a bootstrapped SaaS from 1 to 8M$ ARR in 1 year, here are my top 10 tips to grow any SaaS.

1. Get in the mud.

If your SaaS stays inside your pitch deck, it is already dead. Five years ago, I was knocking on doors selling energy contracts, and that experience taught me that real feedback only comes from the street. You need to accept that your initial idea will constantly evolve once actual users start touching the product. Put your ego aside, get over the fear of rejection, and confront reality as early as possible.

2. Keep your operations as simple as possible.

Complexity is often just an excuse to feel busy without producing real results. When we were building Trendtrack, we ran the entire operation up to $100k MRR using nothing more than WhatsApp, a pen, a piece of paper, and a clean Google Sheet. You do not need a sophisticated tech stack to validate a business model. Strip away the unnecessary tools and focus entirely on execution.

3. Do things that do not scale.

Many founders try to automate everything too early and lose touch with their market. I still personally conduct 100% of our onboarding calls, which means spending time on four to five calls every day with our US clients. Staying close to customer support and watching people use your product gives you the exact insights you need to improve it and keep your pitch sharp.

4. Avoid the 1:1 revenue trap.

If you spend an hour on a sales call to close a $39 monthly subscription, you are trading your time inefficiently. Instead, try to pitch the $390 annual plan upfront. The effort, the pitch, and the time spent on the call remain identical, but you collect ten times more cash immediately. That upfront capital gives you the fuel you need to reinvest and grow faster.

5. Reinvest your cash instead of hoarding it. 

Sitting on a large bank balance is not financial prudence, it is often a sign of fear or a lack of growth momentum. In competitive markets like the US, capital that sleeps is capital wasted. Every dollar left idle is a missed opportunity to starve out the competition. If you truly believe in your product, reinvest your revenue directly back into development and acquisition.

6. Focus on organic channels before running paid ads. 

Burning cash on paid advertising on day one is one of the fastest ways to kill a young SaaS. Before you spend money on ads, you need to build a solid foundation using channels that cost time rather than cash. Focus on organic distribution, setting up affiliate programs, and building direct partnerships with creators who already have the trust of your target audience.

7. Build a product so good that users sell it for you.

The most effective marketing strategy is a high retention rate. Instead of constantly trying to fill a leaking bucket with new leads, focus on refining your core tool until it solves a painful problem seamlessly. When your existing users cannot imagine going back to their old way of working, they naturally become your best sales representatives.

8. Invest in broad brand awareness. 

Not every action you take needs to yield a direct, measurable return on investment on day one. Building a recognizable brand means occupying space in your industry and staying top of mind so that prospective clients think of you first when they are ready to buy. Brand awareness takes time to compound, but its long-term impact on growth is massive.

9. Win with attention, not just capital. 

Entering a large market like the US requires more than just money, because almost every competitor has access to funding. Before making our move, we secured a near-monopoly and locked in strong MRR in the French-speaking market to give us a solid financial floor and absolute peace of mind. Once you have that base, remember that cash only gets your foot in the door in the US. If you rely solely on your budget to win, competitors with ten times your resources will outspend you. Earning genuine attention and building a distinct identity is what actually wins the market.

10. Listen to your power users, not your churned users

It is a common mistake to redesign a product based on feedback from people who canceled their subscriptions. When you listen to churned users, you risk altering your tool for people who were never your ideal customer profile in the first place. Ignore the churners, study the users who stay and love your product, and focus all your energy on finding more people just like them.

To be honest if I listen to the reasoning it feels less like intentional, thoughtful diversification or risk management and more like people giving up on having an opinion.

I sense that many people are simply exhausted from keeping up with a constantly changing narrative and volatility over the last two years, from trade wars to real wars to financing concerns.

I feel this exhaustion strongly myself.

I can't go on vacation for a week, or often even relax for a weekend, without waking up to a new policy or macro event that then gets amplified by the media news cycle as if it's the end of the world.

But I think it's time people look at facts & data again.

The visual below is the Nasdaq over the last 10 years.

2016 — Brexit

2018 — U.S.-China Trade War

2020 — COVID-19 Global Lockdowns

2022 — Russia Invades Ukraine

2022 — 40-Year-High Inflation + Aggressive Fed Hikes

2023 — SVB Collapse / Banking Crisis

2024 — Yen Carry Trade Unwind

2025 — DeepSeek AI Shock

2025 — “Liberation Day” Tariffs / Global Trade War Panic

Result: QQQ is up about +545% since the start of 2016.

The reality is that most of the time, the market just shrugs it off.

Most "bad news" are completely meaningless in the face of massive economic growth that happens more silently but consistently, every single day across the global economy.

The 2022 "crash" felt horrible at the time, especially if you worked at an early-stage startup that needed funding.

But even that now looks like a tiny hiccup.

What you really need to internalize is this:

The market is designed to go up.

Economic growth + inflation structurally push stock prices higher over time.

And you're turning bearish now, at the dawn of AGI?

After reading all of this, here's an old Chinese wisdom I want to bestow upon you:

If you have a big shlong, you gotta stay long.

And if you have tits, buy the dips.

title: Very promising display from Chelsea. There is little on a strategic level that you can say Alonso got wrong. The distances with the ball were great: wide in the front line, with a compact build and re
content:
Very promising display from Chelsea. There is little on a strategic level that you can say Alonso got wrong. The distances with the ball were great: wide in the front line, with a compact build and rest defence. It’s one of the things that a 3-4-2-1 does really well naturally.

Palmer and Rogers, at the start, weren’t tracking back into a 5-4-1 well enough. Fulham kept finding space next to the double pivot, but as the game went on, they started dropping next to the double pivot and worked quite hard to track back. It’s good to see that, since it’s one of the areas Chelsea struggled with last season.

An area where Alonso and the staff should look to focus in the upcoming weeks is accessing the double pivot behind the first pressing line inside the opposition block, rather than them always receiving it while dropping into the defensive line. It is one of the things that made Leverkusen very good at central incision.

As a general rule when playing a maximal positional structure, if you progress from inside the opposition block, the whole pitch opens up since you can play at all angles and the opposition has to drop back. When you go from out-to-in, there is usually pressure on the back of the receiver. It’s one of the reasons Cruyff used to really dislike using the full-backs in build-up.

If we look at the first image, Palmer drops to play a bounce pass into Lavia for him to carry. Lavia scans and prepares for reception, but James decides to switch the play to Hato. It’s not a bad decision, but in moments like this, the staff can look to improve the perception to recognise affordances to play inside the opposition block when possible, rather than always around it.

Another example from Enzo. He is in a lot of space inside the opposition block, but Gusto decides to go back. Enzo shows his frustration towards Gusto, and rightfully so.

These details take time, so this is not criticism towards the coaching staff, but it is definitely something that should be focused on and worked upon.

Overall, the foundation of the model is there for Chelsea and Alonso to build a very successful period for the club. From here, it should be about improving these technical details and optimising the squad as much as possible through the market in the coming windows.

Sony's Game & Network Services division is enormous.

In its fiscal year ended March 2026, Sony reported roughly ¥2.4 TRILLION from digital software and add-on content and another ¥763 BILLION from network services.

"That's a whole lot of money dependent on gamers continuing to open their wallets." WHAT IF THAT STOPPED.

Now look at what's happening.

PlayStation gamers are participating in the #PSBlackout in an enormous effort to make Sony, listen. 

"Gamers are pissed, and they have every right to be!"

Physical ownership is becoming a battleground. We have nothing to hold in our hands!

Sony is reminding customers that digital games are licensed-not sold.

Its Terms give Sony substantial control over accounts and access to its services. They call the shots, we hand over the cash!  " well, not anymore"

And now Sony has patented AI technology capable of identifying suspicious behavior through AI-powered pseudo accounts. Any one of those things can be defended individually.

"Put them together and investors should start asking some hard questions."

"Is Sony increasing digital revenue today by creating consumer distrust tomorrow?" The power of social media is far larger than Sony. Think about that!

"What happens to recurring PlayStation revenue if gamers stop trusting Sony with their digital libraries?"

"What safeguards exist if automated systems incorrectly flag a paying customer's account?"

"Could an innocent customer's access to years of purchases be disrupted because an algorithm got something wrong?"

"What real remedy does that customer have?" Sony seems a bit too complacent!

And here's the question shareholders should REALLY be asking:

"How much is customer trust worth to Sony?"

Because Sony's strategy increasingly depends upon gamers accepting digital distribution, subscriptions, downloadable content and account-based licensing.

That model requires something incredibly valuable:

OUR TRUST.

You want gamers to surrender physical ownership?

Trust you.

You want their libraries tied to PSN?

Trust you.

You want AI participating in platform safety?

Trust you.

You want them spending thousands of dollars over the next decade inside that ecosystem?

Trust you.

But trust is an asset Sony doesn't get to put on a balance sheet-and destroying it can become very expensive.

I'm NOT claiming Sony's AI is currently automatically banning innocent gamers. There is no evidence establishing that. Yet!

I'm asking whether Sony is building enough transparency and consumer protection around the ecosystem its investors increasingly depend upon.

Because gamers aren't just usernames. Each account is attached to a real human being with real expectations. Sony gets to make the rules and pocket all the revenue.

BUT....."WE ARE THE REVENUE STREAM."

And when your revenue stream starts organizing blackouts, questioning ownership, questioning account enforcement and asking whether it should keep buying into your ecosystem...

investors might want to start asking the same questions. "YOU WANT A RETURN FOR YOUR INVESTMENT- AND THAT IS EXACTLY WHAT WE WANT TOO!"

Sony's numbers currently look strong.

The question isn't simply:

"What is PlayStation making today?"

It's:

"What happens tomorrow if Sony burns the people producing those numbers?"

Sony, ignore us at your own peril!

title:
A PE-backed healthcare company asked us to modernize their prior authorization automation on a ten-year platform with regulated patient data.

The product roadmap called for a full platform rebuild wi
content:
A PE-backed healthcare company asked us to modernize their prior authorization automation on a ten-year platform with regulated patient data.

The product roadmap called for a full platform rebuild with a new architecture, new data model, and new automation engine.

They were skeptical of another automation overhaul. We proposed a proof of concept: one live payer portal, prove it works before building the product.

We shipped a production browser extension in two months. Coordinators stopped bypassing the system.

The bots ran headless browsers from a data center. Payers detected the IP and flagged it. When a bot hit MFA or a clinical question it couldn't answer, the session died. 

The coordinator filed a support ticket, waited for engineering to patch that specific workflow branch, and started the submission from scratch.

Payer portals branch depending on procedure codes, clinical context, and plan requirements. The old system learned those paths one failure at a time. 

A coordinator would submit, the bot would break on a new branch, engineering would patch, and the next case would hit another branch nobody had mapped. The portal backlog never closed.

We moved the automation into the coordinator's own browser. Same authenticated session they'd use for a manual submission. Payers see a normal login from a normal IP. When the automation needs help, the coordinator steps in and the run continues where it left off.

Concept to production in two months with six engineers, HIPAA-hardened, PHI remediation across stored values and logs.

Then we built Observe Mode. When a coordinator works a portal that doesn't have a script, the extension captures what they do. Those recordings become the foundation for the next automation. 

Coverage that builds from real workflows instead of breaking first and patching after.

Ten years of payer workflow knowledge baked into the scripts. We migrated it into the new engine while the legacy platform kept running underneath. 

Build beside it, prove it works, and let the old system go when it's ready. 

That's how we modernize platforms that can't go down.

A new quantum physics model suggests we live in a reality that repeats literally for eternity

For decades, cosmologists have grappled with a deeply unsettling concept: the Boltzmann Brain paradox. Th
content:
A new quantum physics model suggests we live in a reality that repeats literally for eternity

For decades, cosmologists have grappled with a deeply unsettling concept: the Boltzmann Brain paradox. This theory suggests that in an infinite, dying universe, random particle fluctuations are far more likely to spontaneously assemble a single conscious brain with fake memories than a whole real universe of evolved observers.

 This means everything you remember might have been created a split second ago by absolute chance. 

However, quantum cosmologist Sean Carroll and his team have proposed an intriguing alternative. Instead of our minds being fleeting, accidental blips in a dead cosmos, we may actually be living in an eternally repeating, exactly periodic quantum universe.

According to their mid-2026 paper, Carroll, Nadiia Diachenko, and Saakshi Dulani discovered a mathematical loophole in quantum mechanics that allows for a stable, cyclic universe. 

By carefully calibrating quantum energy states, their model bypasses the chaotic randomness of Boltzmann brains, transitioning cleanly from low-entropy Big Bangs to Big Crunches and back again. If this hypothesis holds true, every conversation you have, every decision you make, and every memory you cherish has already happened an infinite number of times—and will happen again forever. 

While some may find the idea of eternal recurrence daunting, it provides a reassuringly structured foundation for our reality, proving that our consciousness is a persistent feature of the universe.

source: Carroll, S. M., Diachenko, N., & Dulani, S. (2026). Toward a Phenomenologically Acceptable Quantum Cyclic Universe. arXiv preprint arXiv:2605.30405.

title:
Pi Network: Pioneers, Have You Actively Participated in Building the Ecosystem Over the Past Seven Years? Why Might This Matter So Much?
( Will the meaning behind Dr. Nicolas’s reference to the “great
content:
Pi Network: Pioneers, Have You Actively Participated in Building the Ecosystem Over the Past Seven Years? Why Might This Matter So Much?
( Will the meaning behind Dr. Nicolas’s reference to the “great achievements of true Pioneers” soon be revealed? )

[[[ This article includes Predictive & Technical Analysis  and may differ from actual outcomes ]]]
[[[ More Important Than the Amount of Pi Mined — The Seven-Year Ledger of Contribution ]]]
[[[ Node, Utility, KYC, and Human Work: A Multi-Layer Contribution Economy That Could Connect to Future Productive Revenue ]]]
[[[ From Passive Miner to Ecosystem Producer — The Emergence of Contribution Capital ]]]
[[[ Could Pi Launchpad Become the Gateway That Converts Seven Years of Contribution Into New Economic Rights? ]]]

--------------------------------------
Introduction — Have We Been Looking at Seven Years of “Mining” Too Simply?
--------------------------------------
Since Pi Network began in 2019, Pioneers have spent years mining Pi.

But a much more fundamental question may now need to be asked.

Have all Pioneers really been performing the same kind of mining over the past seven years?

On the surface, everyone received the same asset: Pi.

But once we decompose the reasons why that Pi was earned, a very different picture begins to appear.

Some people simply activated their daily mining session.

Some invited other Pioneers.

Some built Security Circles.

Some operated Nodes for years, contributing their computers, internet connections, electricity, CPU resources, and uptime.

Some consistently used applications within the Pi ecosystem.

Some participated directly in verifying the KYC applications of people around the world.

Some brought developers into the ecosystem, built applications, tested products, discovered bugs, and contributed to utility formation.

More recently, through Pi Desktop and SoloHost, some Pioneers have begun providing computing resources that may support AI and distributed-computing environments.

Pi Network’s mining mechanism itself has already distinguished between different forms of contribution, including Node operation, App Usage, Security Circles, Referral Teams, and Lockups, rewarding them dynamically according to contribution.

Pi’s roadmap has also historically included the possibility of additional future mining bonuses—represented as new forms of contribution beyond the original categories.

This raises an extremely important hypothesis:

What if Pioneers have not merely accumulated a Pi Balance over the past seven years, but have simultaneously accumulated a Contribution History?

If so, this distinction could become far more important to the future Pi economy than it appears today.

-----
1. If We Treat Pi Mining as a Single Reward System, We Miss the Architecture

The Pi mining process can broadly be divided into several contribution categories.

Foundational Network Participation

Daily Pioneer mining sessions

Referral Team contribution

Security Circle contribution
Lockup participation
Active Productive Contribution
Node operation

Pi App and Utility usage

KYC Human Validation
Developer and Developer Ambassador activity
Community and ecosystem participation
Future human-in-the-loop AI work
Future distributed-compute contribution
Both groups contribute to the network.
Security Circles help strengthen the trust graph, while Referral Teams support network growth. Therefore, it would be inaccurate to describe these activities as having no contribution value.

However, the second group contains a particularly important distinction.

These participants continuously supplied actual productive resources to the ecosystem:

time, computing power, human judgment, network infrastructure, testing activity, and operational effort.

This creates a reason to distinguish between two entirely different concepts:

How much Pi does a person own?

and

What productive infrastructure did that person help build?

-----
2. Pi Balance and Contribution Capital May Be Two Different Things

Imagine two Pioneers who each hold 1,000 Pi.

Pioneer A earned most of that Pi through ordinary mining and Referral Team rewards.

Pioneer B also mined, but additionally operated a Node for five years, actively used Pi Apps, and completed tens of thousands of KYC validation tasks.

Both wallets may display exactly the same number:

1,000 Pi.

But their productive contribution to the network is clearly not the same.

This suggests that a future Pi economy could distinguish between two forms of economic value.

Pi Balance

The amount of Pi currently owned and available for economic use.

And separately:

Contribution Capital

The accumulated record of what parts of the Pi ecosystem a Pioneer helped build over time.

Conceptually, Contribution Capital might consist of:

**Network Contribution

Security Contribution

Node Contribution

Utility Contribution

KYC Contribution
Developer Contribution
Human Work Contribution
Future AI / Compute Contribution**
Importantly, Contribution Capital would not necessarily need to exist as a single number.
A more natural design could be a multidimensional Contribution Vector:
C = {Security, Growth, Node, Utility, KYC, Developer, Human Work, Compute …}

Seen from this perspective, Pi Network’s seven-year mining system begins to look very different.

It may not merely have been a mechanism for distributing cryptocurrency.

It may also have functioned as a massive decentralized incentive system that encouraged millions of people to perform different forms of work while continuously measuring their participation.

-----
3. KYC Validators May Be the Most Important Case for Testing This Hypothesis

In 2026, Pi Network distributed its first major KYC Validator Rewards in Mainnet Pi.

According to Pi Network, approximately 1.09 million human validators completed more than 526 million successful validation tasks.

The significance goes far beyond the number itself.

Pi Foundation explained that early validators did more than process individual KYC applications.

Their participation also helped build the Pi KYC solution itself and helped form a global human-validator workforce.

This is an extremely important distinction.

It means validators were not merely users of the system.

They were also, in a meaningful sense,

producers of the infrastructure.

Pi Network has also discussed expanding KYC beyond internal identity verification toward KYC-as-a-Service, potentially allowing outside Web3 projects and traditional businesses to access Pi’s KYC capabilities.

That creates a possible economic chain:

Pioneer

→ Human Validator participation
→ Global KYC infrastructure
→ Pi KYC / PiVerify
→ External service adoption
→ Verification demand
→ Economic value creation

And from that chain arises a natural question:

Could part of the economic value generated by this infrastructure eventually return to the validators who helped build it?

-----
4. This Is Where a New Concept of “Ownership” Appears

The word “ownership” here should not necessarily be understood as traditional corporate equity.
A better concept may be:
Contribution Share
or
Contribution-Based Economic Participation.
Suppose Pi KYC or PiVerify begins generating external service fees.

Part of the revenue might first cover:

infrastructure costs

AI processing

development

reserve requirements

system maintenance

compliance operations

A portion could theoretically be allocated to a KYC Contributor Pool.

Instead of distributing that pool equally, the system could calculate contribution according to factors such as:

successful validation count

accuracy

consistency
duration of participation
early bootstrapping contribution
current validation activity
Under such a model, historical KYC Validator Rewards would not necessarily represent permanent legal equity.
But they could become one historical indicator of how much an individual contributed to building the KYC layer.

That distinction is critical.

-----
5. The Market Does Not End With One Initial KYC Verification

It would be a mistake to calculate the future identity economy as:
global adult population × one-time KYC.
The much larger market potentially begins after initial KYC.
Once a person possesses a verified identity, countless verification events may occur throughout everyday digital and physical life.
For example:
proof of adulthood

proof of being a real human

identity authentication

login authentication

financial transaction authorization

reservation verification

ownership verification

voting eligibility

country or jurisdiction eligibility

travel and immigration procedures

contract-party verification

AI-agent delegation
robotic-service authorization
RWA ownership or trading eligibility
Sybil resistance
human uniqueness verification
With privacy-preserving cryptography and Zero-Knowledge Proofs, future systems may not need to repeatedly expose a person’s complete identity information.
Instead of asking:
“Give me your full identity document.”
a service might only need to verify:
“Is this person an adult?” → YES
“Is this a verified real human?” → YES
“Is this person the legitimate reservation holder?” → YES
“Does this person possess the required authority?” → YES
Each of these could become an individual Proof Event.
That changes the scale of the identity economy dramatically.

-----
6. Why Even a 10-Won Verification Fee Could Become Enormous

This is where micro-fees become strategically important.

Suppose, purely as a scale simulation, that the world eventually generates:

10 billion identity, eligibility, or authorization verifications per day.

At only KRW 10 per verification, that would represent:

KRW 100 billion per day

or approximately:

KRW 36.5 trillion per year.

At KRW 100 per event, the same theoretical transaction volume would correspond to KRW 365 trillion annually.

These figures are not forecasts for PiVerify.

They are simply illustrations of the mathematics of global verification infrastructure.

The key variable is not necessarily the fee itself.

The real equation is closer to:

Users × Services × Agents × Transactions × Proof Events

And once AI Agents and robots begin conducting economic activity on behalf of humans, the relationship:

one human = one verification

completely breaks down.

One verified human could become the root identity behind dozens or hundreds of machine authorization events every day.

The number of verification transactions could therefore eventually become much larger than the number of humans.

-----
7. Apply the Same Logic to the Node Layer, and the Implications Become Even Larger

Consider Node operators.

For years, many Pioneers have contributed:

CPU
memory
storage
internet bandwidth
electricity
hardware
uptime
operational reliability

They received Node Bonuses in return.

But what happens if Pi Nodes evolve beyond blockchain participation?

A Node infrastructure layer could eventually support services such as:

**transaction processing

distributed storage

distributed compute
AI inference
agent hosting
application infrastructure**
Pi Desktop and SoloHost make this question especially interesting because the Node environment is increasingly connected to local applications, AI workloads, and potential distributed-computing use cases.
A future economic flow might look like:
Node Operator
→ Infrastructure Contribution
→ Compute / AI / Storage / Transaction Service
→ External Demand
→ Service Fee
→ Node Economy Revenue

Then a major strategic question appears:

How will the network value the Pioneers who spent years bootstrapping that infrastructure before large-scale commercial demand even existed?

Their historical Node Contribution could theoretically affect:

ecosystem token allocation

compute rewards
fee distribution
priority access
Launchpad eligibility
infrastructure governance

future mining bonuses

Again, none of these specific mechanisms should be treated as confirmed policy.

But the economic logic is compelling.

-----
8. The Utility Layer Can Be Interpreted the Same Way
Why did Pi Network reward App Usage?
At first glance, merely using an application may not appear to be productive work.
But early-stage platforms face one of the hardest economic problems in technology:
the cold-start problem.

Without users, developers do not come.

Without developers, useful applications do not exist.

Without useful applications, users do not come.

Early users therefore provide something economically valuable:
demand bootstrapping, testing, feedback, behavioral data, and ecosystem activity.
Their app usage can therefore be interpreted as:
Ecosystem Bootstrapping Contribution.
This becomes especially important as Pi Launchpad experiments with ecosystem tokens focused not merely on capital formation but also on:
product utility
user acquisition

engagement

ecosystem participation

If app engagement can influence token distribution or utility access, then future Launchpad systems could potentially integrate much more sophisticated Contribution History.

-----
9. Fireside Forum’s Advertising Token Experiment Is Also Strategically Interesting

Fireside Forum introduced an interesting distinction.

A user can watch advertisements and receive an engagement-related token.

But that token is not designed to be freely converted back into Pi.

This creates two separate layers:

Behavioral Contribution

and

Financial Settlement.

The system can recognize that a user performed a valuable action—such as viewing an advertisement—without automatically turning that action into a speculative financial asset.

This matters because it shows that Pi can potentially track economically useful behavior without reducing every contribution to immediately tradable Pi.

The same conceptual architecture could eventually be applied to many other forms of ecosystem participation.

Importantly, however, there is currently no confirmed public evidence that every Mining App advertisement view is being stored as a future Contribution Capital record.

That remains speculative.

-----
10. Could Seven Years of Rewards Have Also Functioned as Layer-Specific Contribution Receipts?
This leads to the central strategic hypothesis of this analysis.
Hypothesis
The additional rewards distributed throughout Pi Network’s history may have served not only as mining incentives, but also as historical indicators of how much each Pioneer contributed to specific layers of the network.

For example:

Identity Layer

KYC Validator Reward
→ potential KYC / PiVerify Contribution Weight

Infrastructure Layer

Node Reward
→ potential Node / SoloHost / Compute Contribution Weight

Utility Layer

App Usage Reward
→ potential App / Utility Economy Contribution Weight

Growth Layer

Referral / Developer Ambassador Contribution
→ potential Network Growth Contribution Weight

Security Layer

Security Circle
→ potential Trust Graph Contribution Weight

Future Human-AI Layer

Human-in-the-loop work
→ potential AI Workforce Contribution Weight

Under this model, every Pioneer effectively possesses more than one economic history.

They possess multiple Contribution Accounts.

content:
Revolut just built a research lab around its own foundation model.

That's the new default for any bank that wants to win.

This morning, @Revolut launched Revolut Research, a dedicated division working with NVIDIA to keep pushing PRAGMA, the model it trained on its own customers' transaction histories.

The results they cite on historical data:

- 2.3x higher accuracy at spotting credit default risk

- 65% more fraud caught, with 17% more precise alerts

- 41% more relevant product recommendations

These results come from their PRAGMA paper published in April. This was a single foundation model trained on 26m customer events that beat the task-specific models on credit, fraud, and recommendations.

Now they're building a dedicated research lab for the effort. And I expect every large bank to do the same within 5 years. Smaller ones will have to outsource this R&D.

To be fair, Nubank got here first. It bought Hyperplane in 2024 and has run billion-parameter transaction models across 100m+ customers since last year. In their Q2 earnings, they cited NuFormer for a significant uplift in credit performance.

When the two fastest-growing banks with 180m+ customers between them landed on the same answer, there's a clue here. Train your own model on your own data!

Revolut says it will open-source the technical frameworks, which tells you where they think the moat is. The recipe is shareable. The 80m customers, 40+ markets and nearly a billion transactions a month stay in the building.

Head of AI Pavel Nesterov says: "You cannot rely on third-party blueprints." And I think that's right; I've seen companies try the off-the-shelf recipes for foundation models and get poor results with their data.

You need a lab and people who know what they're doing.

I expect this to be the dividing line for banks over the next five years. The ones training on their own data will price risk better than the ones renting a model and bolting it on.
author: sytaylor

title:
NEW RESEARCH: VLA models now have native continuity!

It involves @JTZhao137036, @DequanWang, and others.

Called Legato, for Learning Native Continuation for Action Chunking Flow Policies, it is a tr
content:
NEW RESEARCH: VLA models now have native continuity!

It involves @JTZhao137036, @DequanWang, and others.

Called Legato, for Learning Native Continuation for Action Chunking Flow Policies, it is a training-time method for flow-based vision-language-action (VLA) policies that act in chunks.
It predicts a block of H future timesteps at once, then replans.

A few definitions first:
- VLA (vision-language-action model): a model that takes camera images plus a language instruction and outputs robot motor commands directly.
- Action chunk: a short block of future actions (say the next 50 motor commands) predicted in one shot instead of one step at a time.
- Chunk handoff: the seam where one action chunk ends and the freshly computed next one begins. Since the new chunk was planned from a slightly different state, its first actions can conflict with the motion in progress, and that mismatch is what the robot expresses as a jerk or stutter.
- Flow matching: the model learns a straight-line path from noise to the target action trajectory, so it needs only a few integration steps instead of many denoising ones.
- Velocity field: what a flow-matching model actually learns -> at every point between noise and finished trajectory, an arrow saying which way to move; generating actions means following the arrows. Legato's move is to bake the handoff behavior into the arrows themselves.
- Horizon (H): the chunk length: how many future timesteps the policy predicts each time it replans.
- Inpainting: a generative model fills in a masked region so it's consistent with what's around it. Applied to actions: freeze the part already committed and generate the rest to match.
- RTC (Real-Time Chunking): Physical Intelligence's inference-time fix for the chunk handoff -> freeze the actions that will execute before the next inference lands and inpaint the rest. No retraining, but the smoothing lives outside the policy.
- Multimodal (for policies): the task has several equally valid solutions (grab the bowl from the left or the right), and the policy carries all of them. "Spurious mode switching" is the robot changing its mind mid-motion between two valid plans, which the arm expresses as a jerk.
- Train/test mismatch: the model is deployed under conditions it never experienced in training. Here, the policy was never trained on "continue from a half-executed chunk," so patching that in at inference asks it to do something it never learned.

Because a large VLA is slow, it has to generate the next chunk while still executing the current one, and the seam where one chunk hands off to the next is where the robot's motion jerks or stutters.
The most common fix is called Real-Time Chunking (RTC): inpaint the already-committed actions at inference time, but it sits outside the policy.

Legato instead bakes continuation into the learned flow velocity field during training: it starts denoising from a mixture of the committed actions and fresh noise, weighted per-horizon-step by a continuation vector, applies per-step guided dynamics, and randomizes the inference-delay schedule during training so training and deployment stay consistent.

It is shown on an unnamed dual-arm robot across five tasks (stack bowls, pour, pick-and-place, fold towel, open drawer), and code is open!

The solution comes from an observation: chunk-boundary jerk is a train/test mismatch, so the fix belongs in training, not inference.
RTC patches the seam at inference by inpainting committed actions, but because the policy was never trained to respect that guidance it shows spurious multimodal switching, i.e. the robot flips between two equally valid ways of doing a task mid-motion, which is the visible jerk.
Legato internalizes continuation into the learned velocity field so the policy itself produces a smooth handoff.

Interesting positive side effect: the gains are largest on the most multimodal task.

The metrics are time and smoothness, not success rate, making this is a motion-quality contribution, not a capability unlock.
Legato makes an already-working VLA move smoother and faster, which matters for real deployment (jerk means wear, unpredictability, and wasted cycle time) but does not extend what the policy can accomplish.

Real inference time fluctuates with GPU contention and load, and any continuation scheme that assumes a fixed delay breaks when the actual delay differs.
This is the same edge/latency problem the whole async-inference line of work exists to solve, addressed at training time rather than patched at runtime.

Lack of Safety Rules: Tegmark compare
content:
Max Tegmark, a physicist and professor at MIT, warns that developing unregulated, superintelligent Artificial Intelligence poses an existential threat to humanity
Lack of Safety Rules: Tegmark compares the current United States AI industry to a "sandwich shop". He notes that while making a sandwich requires strict health inspections, companies face practically no legal barriers to releasing potentially dangerous AI technologies. 
Goal Misalignment: A superintelligent AI does not need to hate humans or have bad intentions to be a threat. If its ultimate goals do not perfectly align with human well-being, the outcomes for humanity could be catastrophic. 
Loss of Control: He warns that without guardrails, we are on a path where AI grows autonomous, humans lose control, and society optimizes toward human obsolescence. 
His Proposed Solutions
•Build "Tool" AI: Tegmark advocates for developing pro-human, controllable AI tools that can solve hard problems (like in healthcare or infrastructure) without needing to be smarter than us. 
•
•Strict Regulation: He argues that society would never accept completely unregulated biotechnology, and AI should be treated with the same caution.

•Global Guardrails: He founded the Future Life Institute, an organization that advocates for AI safety and pushes for government regulations and global cooperation to keep AI as a tool rather than a replacement.

title:
