I'll explain in more detail, and then
content:
I really didn't expect this to get as much circulation as it did, but then again looking back, it's always the least-legible things that people get crazy about.

I'll explain in more detail, and then maybe we can have some more informed arguments.

First, the quoted post is not based on observations about the US.

This is based on observations of China, which I consider to be the world's most advanced economy, where "advanced" is measured by "furthest up the Kardashev scale." The US (esp tech) might think it's further along, but 1) that AI lead is very small, and 2) Kardashev is measured primarily by amount of usable energy harnessed. China is far beyond the US on that front.

(If you don't agree, you can click [x] and unfollow)

There are two things we often hear about China:

1) China is facing a population bomb, with plummeting fertility rates and not enough young people to support its elderly population!
2) China has too many people, its youth unemployment rate is super high (~18% in July 2026)!

How can a country have too few young people and too many young people at once?

The answer could be one of any number of economic theories. Here's a new one, which is what I was thinking in my original post:

(This isn't a well-developed theory - the Rats call it a "butterfly idea" - so you've been warned)

Once of the nuances about China's youth unemployment isn't that the jobs don't exist, it's that many unemployed youth don't want to work the jobs that do exist. 

One emerging scenario is this: there are many jobs available, but they either pay too little or are uninteresting, and young people prefer to just live with their parents instead of spending their time working one of those jobs. Although China does not have a big welfare system, their parents happen to own enough savings and assets that they are able to pay for their [one] child to continue living with them.

Notice the interesting inversion here: the prior assumption about "one child supporting two parents and four grandparents" inverts to "two parents support just one child."

(There's the "four grandparents" but there are not necessarily four living grandparents, and many old people live very cheaply)

That prior assumption rested on yet another assumption, which is that, as a general rule, people would not have substantial retirement assets and so one's children were one's retirement plan: a productive child is the person supporting their elderly indigent parents. 

Children do still often support their parents, but another thing may also be happening: parents save enough assets to fund their retirement, and the assets grow faster than they use them, especially as they scale back the cost of their lifestyle, and - in some cases - it ends up being enough to continue supporting their child.

The scenario I describe would occur more often if the cost of living stayed low or even dropped over time.

Again, this is a China effect: China's industrial policy does not focus on maximizing profits (or GDP), but rather on what we might call "make more stuff and everything gets cheaper."

Everyone versed in economics understands this notion; we have lots of arguments in SF about "build more housing if you want it to be cheaper, and so more people can have housing."  

Well, China produces more of everything, especially the things needed for regular living: consumer goods, groceries, etc. It drives prices down by encouraging producers to hyperscale production, and while this does not maximize profits, they more or less "make it up on volume." The West imagines this to be some kind of nefarious predatory strategy to destroy Western industries, but it's really just China making more because when everyone has more, the people are happy.

The US company that comes closest to this philosophy is Amazon, which famously optimizes for scale and operational efficiency so as to maximize value delivered to customers, putting price pressure on its suppliers and keeping their operating margin razor-thin (excludes digital services like AWS). Amazon's competitors also think that it's a nefarious predatory strategy to destroy them, but it's just Amazon serving the most customers at the lowest possible prices!

Here's a question: if post-scarcity abundance was on the way, what would be the first signs?

Well, you might see a lot of overproduction (or overcapacity). And that would tend to drive prices towards zero.

In the US we often focus on the jobs effect of that: your labor will be worth nothing, so you're going to lose your job. Well okay, but all the shit you need to buy also becomes free. How much do you need a job if everything you need is free?

That argument obscures the weird part by pointing at the ends: the weird bit is in the transitionary middle, where you've lost your job, things are very-cheap-but-not-free, and you are able to hustle a bit of money with your part-time job.

The economy is not one homogenous good, it's a heterogenous set of goods. But if the production cost of a large enough segment of material goods and daily necessities is driven down far enough, then at some point your overall cost-of-living is falling, not rising.  There are Baumol goods, but they are not intractable - some are due to regulations (very different in China vs what US thinkers are familiar with here).  Example: medical costs are far lower in China, with comparable or superior quality - a big portion of high US medical costs have to do with simple medical supplies in the US being overly expensive.

So you have a situation where elderly parents start from a sufficiently stable financial base where they were already taking care of their grandparents and one child, and then one or more grandparents pass, and their own lifestyle starts to scale back as they age, while cost of living for basic necessities drops over time.  The child is used to a certain standard of living, that standard gets cheaper to maintain, so understandably the child not going to take a job unless they are hyper-ambitious or the job is very interesting and pays super-well.

In the US we are used to thinking of all Asians as hard-working and ambitious, but there are plenty of losers and middling young people in China - they are the ones who are living at home and not going to Tsinghua or Stanford. China has plenty of NEETs. I'm also not saying what I've described above is happening with all of them, but it being true for even 5-10% would yield the high youth unemployment number.

One of the common answers to the declining population "problem" in China is "we'll fill the labor gap with robots." China is indeed far ahead of the US when it comes to robotics. But it hasn't yet reached the level of overhauling society yet (I feel like it could within 2 years...), and the trends I've described have been playing out for at least a decade already.

So, when I say "post-scarcity abundance actually begins by manifesting first as youth unemployment," that is what I'm gesturing at.

The reason it's not manifesting as "everyone unemployment" (...for now) is really just inertia: if you're an older person with a job, you tend to keep that job. It's easier to keep a job than for an entry-level young person to get a new job, especially if that young person isn't looking for any shitty job, but a job that's more interesting and pays significantly more, vs living at home and chilling out.  

Thus, if you have a situation where the segment of the population that finds it hardest to lands a job receives (via whatever combination of events) enough of the economic surplus (in China's case via their parents) that's being created by technologically-driven government-incentivized industrial and agricultural policy focused primarily are reducing scarcity for as many people as possible... then it might mean that the closer you get to post-scarcity abundance, the more those people aren't going to have jobs.

Or more precisely, the more they are going to choose not to take any of the jobs currently available.

Is any of this playing out in the US?

I had lots of comments in my original post lambasting what I said (fair; it's not like I explained anything) from an assumed US standpoint.

The US is a little different. It does not directly focus its economy on maximizing productive output for the broadest possible base of consumers.

It tends to bring (or has historically brought) great prosperity to a great many, but mainly via the indirect effects of capitalism. However, the American system today suffers from a combination of misguided regulation, and profit-optimizing market structuring by large players.

(Here, people like to quibble so here are some caveats; if you find such things tiresome, skip the next three paragraphs:

No, not all regulation is misguided. Some regulation is good and promotes healthier markets and better net outcomes. But good regulation can become out of date, or regulatory capture happens, or dumb regulations get made by officials who are out of touch with technical realities - this last one does seem more and more common.

Large players seek to re-structure the market in ways that are favorable to their profits, and not necessarily total value delivered to customers, e.g. hedge funds buying up all fire engine manufacturers, so that US municipalities have to pay $1-2m for a new truck, while the equivalents can be found on Alibaba for 1/10th the price.

Another example of large market players influencing market structure to optimize for profits is offshoring all of their manufacturing capability!)

Back to the main thread: For many complex and inter-related reasons, cost of living in the US is not falling - it's rising almost untenably for most.

At the same time, it's still hard for young people to find jobs, because the "there are jobs, just not ones I want to take" effect also exists here, except that living with parents or on minimal income is far harder, so everything feels extra shitty. 

When you don't have a job, and everything is very-cheap-but-not-free, BUT you don't have access to those very cheap foreign-made goods because importers buy low and sell high to you while you still only have minimal income, "lying flat" feels like a whole different story in the US, vs China.

One area where a China-like effect does occur is in availability of consumer tech devices.  Tech companies have engaged somewhat more often in the "make more and make it cheaper so more people can buy it" strategy, though this seems to be driven more by the megalomania of creating the biggest possible company than any notion of broad-based industrial economic development - but the effect is similar: almost everyone now carries around a device in their pocket 100x more powerful than the computers on the Saturn V, and has access to untold amounts of online services. America has post-scarcity abundance in a narrow slice of goods and services.

America (or its population) could participate in the Chinese-driven post-scarcity trend by simply  eliminating the trade barriers and allowing Chinese goods to flood the US. And unlike the cheap low-quality Chinese goods of yesteryear (i.e. most Americans' received impression), these are goods of comparable or higher quality.

The problem is that not only would this potentially yield the same "lying flat" youth unemployment issue in the US, it would utterly demolish many American businesses, and thus the wealth base of most American elites. Every American car company would probably be gone in 18 months. And American youth are not going to rebuild America's manufacturing base, they're just not going to. And American robots aren't going to either, they'll be outcompeted by Chinese robots.

In another post, I offhandedly mentioned that we're in the Singularity. Most people who follow me live in the tech sphere, so this was largely accepted unchallenged. But many of the "no we're not" objections basically rested on the idea that "life is still shitty and it's trending worse and the Singularity is supposed to be like Heaven, so we can't possibly be in the Singularity."

Well, there is nothing that says the Singularity or even the post-scarcity abundance world is going to subjectively feel great, much less the transitionary path to it.

The Singularity only says that AI will become smarter than humans, and post-scarcity abundance only says that all material goods are going to be free. Human happiness and pleasure are a function of many things, and most of them are not material. "All your stuff being free and every robot is way smarter than me" does not by itself a utopia make.

The road to post-scarcity abundance is not necessarily going to be a pleasant or positive experience. We still have to choose to make it so.

The rest is left as an exercise to the reader.

title:
Hi, Kevin. International law prof + retired combat soldier/military lawyer @USArmy here.

I watched the show, too. If you're genuinely curious about the discrepancy between @billmaher & some groups/ag
content:
Hi, Kevin. International law prof + retired combat soldier/military lawyer @USArmy here.

I watched the show, too. If you're genuinely curious about the discrepancy between @billmaher & some groups/agencies on the "genocide" issue, read on. You may not hear back from Bill, but I am glad to bring focus to the discrepancy between Bill's correct opinion & that of "some groups and agencies" that "are in disagreement."

To start, let's recap what Bill said in case not everyone did see the show in question.

This was an episode of Real Time with Bill Maher that aired @hbomax this past Friday (8/21). His guests for this segment were @DanaBashCNN & @nytimes reporter Jeremy Peters. For reference, video for the full episode is available @YouTube here (HBO Max subscription required): https://t.co/lVLMDfWtuh) & audio is available @Spotify here: https://t.co/lv1p9ROIxL & @ApplePodcasts here: https://t.co/L6P91PLfUn.

For ease of reference & analysis, though, I've added the clip in question as the first attachment to this post.

As you can see, Bill is talking about the current situation in @TheDemocrats party. On that subject, he says, "They think Gaza is a genocide. It is not. There's an actual meaning [for] the word 'genocide.' It doesn't come close." This discussion continues for another minute or so, and his guests Dana & Jeremy join in on occasion.

What we don't see in this clip is an explanation for what you refer to as a discrepancy between Bill's view & that of "some groups & agencies" to which you refer.

That's the point of the rest of this post - to fill in that gap that doesn't get addressed in Bill's commentary.

The short answer for clarifying the discrepancy can be summarized in just 2 words: sources & methodology. Allow me to explain.

Regarding sources, you need to be aware - if you're not already - that the primary source for establishing international law is ... nations. It's right there in the name: interNATIONal law - or law between nations.

And this is probably so elementary it doesn't need to be said, but I'll say it anyway: "some groups & agencies" are not nation-states.

At best, groups like @amnesty & @hrw & @genocidestudies (which prudently nuked its account after it released the ill-advised "resolution" referred to in the screenshot of what appears to be the Google AI search results you included with your post) qualify as subsidiary sources of international law.

So, there isn't actually a "consensus" among such groups. The only people who claim otherwise are those who selectively highlight the groups that have claimed @Israel is responsible for #genocide in #Gaza while ignoring the experts & groups who have determined otherwise.

Even so, citing to findings of these groups - regardless of where they land on the genocide issue - represents a fundamental misunderstanding regarding how interNATIONal law is formed.

If we stick to the primary source of international law - you know, actual nations - only about 1 in 3 @UN Member States have publicly announced or concluded there is/was genocide in Gaza. Specifically, that's 64 out of 193 UN Member States that have made that determination. 129 have either announced their determination that there is NO genocide or they haven't taken a public stance on the issue (most of the latter are waiting for the final judgement in RSA v. Isr @CIJ_ICJ, which likely won't be reached for several years).

And how do we know that only 64 of 193 UN Member States have publicly announced a "genocide" determination? Easy. I counted.

64 represents the most generous tally I could possibly develop, and it is still only about 33% of UN Member States (pic 1, and it's a number I assess will reduce even more since I conducted the count about 2 months ago since many of these announcements were made for political reasons & domestic politics in several states have shifted from liberal to conservative since then).

Ok, that's the full explanation for the first word in the short answer: sources. You're referring strictly to subsidiary sources as evidence of a "discrepancy" between Bill's view & that of "some groups & agencies." But if you refer to the primary source of international law, you'll notice there is no discrepancy at all. In fact, there is a "discrepancy" between states & this collection of "yes, genocide" groups & agencies to which you refer.

And that brings us to the second word in the short answer: methodology.

You see, the decisive element in determining whether a genocide has been committed typically involves intent. And assessing 🇮🇱 intent is where these "yes, genocide" groups & agencies go astray.

Almost always, they correctly articulate the standard for genocidal intent. We can find that right there in the Genocide Convention.

In case you're not aware, "genocide" involves committing specified acts "with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial or religious group, as such" (pic 2).

Now, here's the methodology these groups & agencies adopt without exception. They refer to a carefully-selected sampling of commentary from certain 🇮🇱elected officials - often mistranslated, misrepresented, or taken out of context - to establish what they claim to be intent to destroy Palestinians, as an identity group, in whole or in part, as such.

For example, they point to a comment from @yoavgallant on 9 Oct 2023 - just 2 days after the 10/7 terror attacks - saying @IDF is fighting against "human animals." However, it's clear from the context that Gallant was referring to Hamas, not the Palestinian population as a whole.

There's also a quote from @IsraeliPM @netanyahu that is always cited in which he says, during remarks televised on 28 Oct 2023, "Remember what Amalek did to you."

For those who aren't familiar, this is a reference to Deuteronomy 25:17–19, which says: "Remember what Amalek did to you on your journey, after you left Egypt — how, undeterred by fear of God, he surprised you on the march, when you were famished and weary, and cut down all the stragglers in your rear. Therefore, when the Eternal your God grants you safety from all your enemies around you, in the land that the Eternal your God is giving you as a hereditary portion, you shall blot out the memory of Amalek from under heaven. Do not forget!"

So, this excerpt from this televised address is almost always referred to as "evidence" that Netanyahu's intent is to destroy Palestinians, in whole or in part, as such.

The problem is (one problem among many, actually), this Amalek reference is taken out of context. Because here's what Netanyahu also says during these remarks: "Yesterday evening, additional ground forces of ours entered the gates of Gaza, at the doorstep of the fortress of evil. This is the second stage of the war, the goals of which are clear: Destroying Hamas's military and governing capabilities, and bringing the captives back home" (full speech available here: https://t.co/2qH3PJZvC0)

Notice the part I emphasized with bold + italics text there? The goal of the campaign is clear: destroy Hamas & bring home all hostages. And this is the part that all these groups & agencies conveniently leave out.

In fact, returning all hostages (which has now been completed) & ending the enduring security threat posed by Hamas have been the stated strategic objectives of the military campaign in Gaza all along. To expand on the goals expressed in the "Amalek" speech in late October 2023, Netanyahu also indicated on the 2 year anniversary of 10/7 that the "aims of the war" are to "return all the hostages, destroy the Hamas regime, and ensure that Gaza no longer poses a threat to Israel" (pic 3).

With that stated strategic intent in mind, do you think intending to destroy a transnational terrorist group - Hamas - in whole, if necessary, in order to end the enduring security threat posed by said terrorist group qualifies as genocide? No. That is war.

And this is where the methodology of all these "yes, genocide" groups & agencies is fundamentally flawed. They fail to start with the actual stated intent of the military campaign in Gaza then assess whether the conduct of the campaign is consistent with that intent or, instead, the intent is to destroy Palestinians as an identity group in whole or in part as such?

At this point, you might be asking why they don't adopt a doctrinal methodology to assessing intent. The answer to that question is simple. Because if they evaluated intent properly, they wouldn't reach the conclusion they want to and seek to reach.

Instead, they would agree with Bill Maher. It's not a genocide, and "it doesn't come close."

Of course, I'm not here to speak for Bill Maher. But if you are genuinely curious why there is such a "discrepancy" between his view and that of the "groups and agencies" to which you refer - that is the answer.

Sources, and methodology. If the reason why that is the case isn't clear from the analysis above, I would be glad to continue this exchange - whether in public or in private.

This scandalous statement was mad
content:
META'S CHIEF SCIENTIFIC ADVISOR, YANN LECUN, SAID, "CHATGPT, CLAUDE, AND ALL CURRENT LANGUAGE MODELS ARE A DEAD END, AND INVESTORS ARE WASTING TRILLIONS OF DOLLARS."

This scandalous statement was made by a Turing Award winner and a man considered one of the "godfathers" of modern AI, which has the entire IT industry in stitches.

While IT giants are buying up hundreds of thousands of NVIDIA graphics cards and promising "superintelligence by next year," LeCun is blunt: attempting to create strong artificial intelligence (AGI) based on LLM is a fundamental misconception for the entire industry.

Here are four compelling arguments from an AI legend about why the chatbot era has hit a wall:

• Lack of a model of the real world: A 4-month-old baby or a cat understands physics, gravity, and space better than the most powerful neural network. Training AI solely on text is like trying to learn to drive by forcing a person to read the instructions on the couch.

• The Illusion of Reason Instead of Thinking: Current LLMs are simply mathematical next-word predictors (pattern matching). They lack logic, true memory, and planning ability. The models produce plausible text, but have no understanding of its semantic essence.

• The Scaling Wall: Increasing data centers and budgets by 10x yields only a symbolic increase in quality. The industry is trying to squeeze the maximum out of a technology that has reached its architectural limits.

• The Shift to "World Models": True AGI will emerge not from text chats, but from fundamentally new architectures-"world models"-capable of perceiving physical reality and cause-and-effect relationships, just as the human brain does.

title:
Today I found yet another reason why EU will lose the AI race and it will remain a renter class to USA.

I work at a university in Finland, EU. Our firewall is blocking access to popular Chinese AI ch
content:
Today I found yet another reason why EU will lose the AI race and it will remain a renter class to USA.

I work at a university in Finland, EU. Our firewall is blocking access to popular Chinese AI chat services like Deepseek and Qwen, but it allows access to OpenAI ChatGPT, Google Gemini, XAI Grok and of course all social  Western social media. And it did allow access to Kimi.

The reason is probably the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) compliance and where your data goes when you type a prompt or attach a file.  

Data Storage Outside the EEA: DeepSeek’s privacy policy has historically disclosed that user data and metadata (like IP addresses and location) are stored on servers in China.

Transferring EU citizens' data outside the European Economic Area (EEA) without specific, legally binding safeguards is a violation of GDPR. 

But this should be in my opinion for users to decide, instead of institution wide bans. Unpublished research is something I would advice to give any chat service, but students using AI to search relevant data from the public net is another story. Currently the latter seems banned as well, at least if you would attempt to do it via Qwen or Deepseek.

Secondly both Qwen and Deepseek are more or less open that they using the free chat user interactions to train their models, same for their free Openrouter models. This is however also the benefit of their model users as the models are open sourced with permissible license. Anybody, including the European institutions can post train and take advantage of the Chinese open source. 

So the European academic institutions are probably honestly believing that the American closed source AI companies are neither using their data for training and handling it safely inside EU servers, even when data is actually also being sent all the USA.

But American closed source models remain closed. Any data you sent to Grok or OpenAI doesn't make the open source models better.

Secondly EU institutions are widely using American operating system (Windows, Android etc), Google services (Google search, Gmail, Google Docs), American app stores, Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, YouTube etc. How naive must a so called data security expert to be that these are probably the biggest spy thing ever face Europeans?

But sure, let's EU continue its current path - let's block the Chinese. 

So far I haven't seen any single European university really getting serious about open source AI. Yes some individuals use it, but that's it. Surprisingly many are using paid Microsoft Copilot. Yes, imagine trying to do state of the art research with the help of Copilot (!!!).

title:
I’ve just spent hours responding to an avalanche of comments about the ChatGPT plugin for Apple Messages. Here are the main ones:

💬 "Anyone can screenshot your messages"

Yes. They can also print the
content:
I’ve just spent hours responding to an avalanche of comments about the ChatGPT plugin for Apple Messages. Here are the main ones:

💬 "Anyone can screenshot your messages"

Yes. They can also print them and fax them to the FBI. People using end to end encryption accept the risk that another participant can deliberately betray their trust. They don’t expect that person to give third party software ongoing access to read, search and analyse their private conversations.

💬 "I opted in, so it’s not a problem"

You opted in. Everyone you communicate with didn’t.

💬 "The encryption still works, so you’re wrong"

Yes, the cryptography still works. My concern is third party access to the readable content before or after decryption.

💬 "The recipient could always share your messages"

Yes. The recipient could betray your trust. That doesn’t justify automating third party access to your private conversations.

💬 "Any Mac app with Full Disk Access could already do this"

Yes. Apple specifically warns that Full Disk Access can expose Messages. OpenAI has now productised that capability for ordinary people who aren't aware of the potential implications, at scale. I don't think Apple saw this coming.

💬 "This is no different from giving AI access to email, SMS, Slack or Teams"

It is. Those services don’t provide the same end to end encryption model as iMessage. Think Signal, not SMS. This Proton, not Gmail.

The screenshot one is my favourite.

I’ll either update my original article with an FAQ or write a dedicated follow up. Thankfully, these comments represent less than 2% of the responses I’ve received here. I haven’t even looked at LinkedIn yet.

My concern with this implementation is scale. One person can enable it on their Mac and expose accessible conversations involving potentially hundreds of people who never enabled ChatGPT, never agreed to the access and aren’t notified. Depending on their Apple and iCloud configuration, that can include historical conversations, participant identifiers, contact information and attachments.

Proton summarised my argument well after reading the article. I recommend reading their post first, then clicking through to mine for the full analysis.

My Substack is free. I’m building a community around corporate surveillance, government overreach, privacy and personal digital safety.

I’m interested in what the technology can do, what information it can access, who else can be affected and what happens when that capability is deployed at scale.

MiniMax H3のプロンプトを作りました。
プロンプトの冒頭で好きな文字に変えて使えるようにしてあります。

最近、H3をずっと使っていてわかってきたのですがプロンプトを書き込むより、ある程度H3に任せちゃってガチャを楽しんだ方が、こういうプロンプトは面白いです。
今回は、かなり文字を削ったので3000文字もないです。

また、完全にテキストだけで作れますのでコピペで簡単にモーショングラフィックが作れます。
何かのオープニングとかタイトルロゴを出すとかMVとか色々と使い道があるんじゃないでしょうか？

段々、わかってきたので、またこのシリーズを続けられたらいいなと考えています。

因みに今回はDomo AIのMiniMax H3 (2k)で生成しました。
ちょっと生成が遅い気がしたのですが、仕上がりはすごく綺麗な気がします。

------------
プロンプト
------------
subject_definitions:
この映像の設定は以下の通りである。
アクセント色は彩度の高いオレンジである。
第1の文字列は "MiniMax H3" である。
第2の文字列は "MOTION" である。
第3の文字列は "GRAPHICS" である。
第4の文字列は "NO EDIT" である。
第5の文字列は "ONE SHOT" である。
第6の文字列は "コピペで" である。
第7の文字列は "超簡単！" である。
第8の文字列は "ONEROOM" である。
第9の文字列は "AI STUDIO" である。
画面を3分割する縦棒は、第1の文字列に含まれる大文字 H の縦棒である。

画面に登場する文字列は上の9つだけであり、これ以外の文字・単語・記号・数字は一切出現しない。すべて上に書いた通りの綴りで、大文字と小文字の別も空白の有無もそのまま正確に保ち、平坦・鮮明・安定した状態で描画する。崩れたり、文字が増減したり、文字化けしたりすることは決してない。
「第1の文字列」「第2の文字列」などの呼び方は、この指示書の中だけで使う呼称である。画面に描くのは必ずその呼称に割り当てられた文字列そのものであり、「第1」「文字列」といった呼称の語や数字が画面に描かれることは決してない。
書体は太いジオメトリックサンセリフ1種類のみで、欧文はすべて大文字。ただし固有名詞にもともと小文字が含まれる場合は、その混在をそのまま正確に保つ。日本語は太いゴシック体1種類のみ。
色はオフホワイト、インクブラック、アクセント色の3色のみ。この3色以外は一切使わない。地の色は映像の途中で白と黒のあいだで3回反転し、そのたびに文字色も反転する。
画面には常に3つの層がある。奥の背景層、中間の装飾層、手前の文字層。この3層は必ず異なる速度で動き、3層すべてが同時に静止する瞬間は最後のホールドだけである。
背景層には第8の文字列が、塗りのない輪郭線だけで描かれ、画面幅の3倍の大きさで横倒しに寝そべり、右から左へ超低速で流れ続けている。これは背景の壁紙であり、手前の文字層とは別物である。重複した単語ではない。
中間の装飾層には、細いバーコードの帯、極小のUIティックの列、レジストレーションマーク、ハーフトーンのドット網、テクニカルな円弧、データ数値のティックが常時いずれか複数存在し、文字層とは別の速度で動いている。

summary:
15秒の爆発的なフラットグラフィック・モーションデザイン。9つのカットすべてが構図的に全く異なり、地の白黒が3回反転し、背景の巨大なアウトライン文字が全編流れ続ける。文字は硬い物体として叩きつけられ、圧縮され、砕け、跳ね返り、増殖し、最後に激突する。ばらばらの線分が第1の文字列を組み上げ、縦棒が画面を3分割し、第2の文字列が叩き込まれ、第3の文字列がワイヤーフレームのグリッド上で増殖し、カードが連打され、収束した光点から第8の文字列が左右から激突して生まれ、最後に第9の文字列を上、第8の文字列を下に置いた2行のロックアップで着地する。

retention_analysis:
各文字列が出現するショットは次の通りであり、増殖・複製された文字もすべて同じ綴りを保つ。
第1の文字列は [Shot 2]、[Shot 3]、[Shot 4] に出現する。
第2の文字列は [Shot 5] に出現する。
第3の文字列は [Shot 6] に出現する。
第4、第5、第6、第7の文字列は [Shot 7] に出現し、いずれも完全に読める状態で保持される。
第8の文字列は背景層に全編出現し、手前の文字層としては [Shot 8]、[Shot 9] に出現する。背景層のものは輪郭線のみ、手前のものは塗りつぶしであり、同じ綴りだが別の層である。誤って重複した単語として扱わない。
第9の文字列は [Shot 9] に出現する。

detailed_description:
本映像は高密度で攻撃的なフラットグラフィックモーションデザインである。エネルギーはすべてタイポグラフィの物理から生み出す。9つのショットはすべて構図が異なっていなければならず、同じ構図、同じスケール、同じ配置を二度使わない。各ショットの演出の細部はここでは指定しない。

[Shot 1] 地は黒。黒い線分の群れが四辺すべてから爆発的に飛び込み、渦を巻きながら中央へ加速して吸い込まれていく。巨大なアクセント色の円が画面外から叩きつけられて着弾し、強いインパクトシェイクが走る。

[Shot 2] At 00:01.000, 渦の中心で線分が一斉に噛み合い、第1の文字列が画面いっぱいに組み上がる。組み上がった瞬間、地が黒から白へ一気に反転する。第1の文字列の最後の1字だけがアクセント色である。

[Shot 3] At 00:02.600, スナップズームでそのアクセント色の1字へ急速に寄り、その1字が画面全体を覆い尽くすまで巨大化する。画面全体が一度だけフリーズする。

[Shot 4] At 00:03.400, 地は白。縦棒が上下へ伸び上がって画面の全高を貫き、画面を3つの縦列に切り分ける。第1の文字列の残りの文字は左へ弾き飛ばされて画面外へ消える。3つの縦列はそれぞれ異なる速度で上下にスクロールする。

[Shot 5] At 00:05.200, 3つの縦列が一斉に急停止し、第2の文字列が画面いっぱいに正面から叩き込まれ、完全に読める状態で静止する。

[Shot 6] At 00:06.400, ハードカットで黒地へ反転する。巨大な白いワイヤーフレームのグリッドが3次元的に傾きながら奥へ伸び、その面に沿って第3の文字列が格子状に増殖して手前へ流れてくる。

[Shot 7] At 00:08.000, グラフィックカードが4枚、ハードカットで連打される。1枚ごとに構図もスケールも配置も異なり、第4、第5、第6、第7の文字列が1枚に1つずつ、画面の中央に大きく現れる。各カードの切り替わりはシャッターフラッシュで区切られる。

[Shot 8] At 00:10.000, 4枚のカードが中央へ一気に吸い込まれ、1つのアクセント色の光点に凝縮する。光点から左右へ、第8の文字列が2つの塊に分かれて超高速で飛び込み、画面中央で激突して一行に綴られる。アクセント色の同心円の衝撃波が中央から外へ炸裂し、砕けた平面の破片がガラスのように四方へ飛び散る。

[Shot 9] At 00:12.000, 破片が画面外へ抜け、第8の文字列が画面の下半分へ落下して着地し、その真上により小さいサイズで第9の文字列が固定される。2行が中央揃えで積み重なる。地が黒から白へ最終反転する。2行のあいだに短いアクセント色の罫線が1本割り込む。00:13.800 から 00:15.000 まで、背景層も含めて画面上のすべてが一切動かない状態を保持する。字形がランダムにグリッチすることは決してない。

キャラクターの膨大な設定と、それを遵守させるための機能でかなりの割合を消費している

自由度と世界観を両立させるゲームデザインだと毎ターン重めのコストが積もっていく

自社環境や、腕利きの本職エンジニアの人達の最適化があればもっと下げれるとは思うけど、商売としての利益とクリエイターへの還元がある前提で考えるなら、あの追加料金は良心的な方なのではないかと思う

ただ、課金導線がダークパターンなのが印象として良くない、そこだけは残念に思う

content:
Elsevierも生成AIの利用方針を更新しました．

結論，
論文執筆でAIを使うこと自体は禁止されていません．

むしろ，
・文献の要約
・研究ギャップの探索
・アイデア出し
・文章構成
・英語や読みやすさの改善
などへの活用は認められています．

ただし，重要なのはここ👇
① AIの出力は必ず人が確認する
② 文献・引用は自分で検証する
③ substantiveな文章修正にはAI使用を開示する
④ 研究方法・解析にAIを使ったらMethodsに記載する
⑤ AIを著者にはできない
⑥ 査読原稿を一般的なAIにアップロードしない
⑦ AIで作った説明図は開示が必要

さらに意外だったのが，
フローチャートや模式図などの説明用画像はAI利用可．
一方で，
顕微鏡画像，組織画像，Western blot，患者画像などの研究データ画像をAIで生成・改変するのはNG．

そして，一般的な生成AIで
Graphical Abstractを作ることも認められていません．

AIを使ったかどうかより，
「何に使い，誰が責任を持つのか」

これが，これからの論文執筆では重要になりそうです．

①実績の整理

content:
AI使わないと置いてかれる…
でも絵に使いたくない…
というイラストレーターさんに、僕がクリエイティブ以外で使い倒してるAIの使い方を⑩個シェアしたいと思います💡
真似できそうなものがあれば是非パクってください！
（ここで言ってるAIは主にClaudeCodeです）

①実績の整理
過去の制作実績を把握してもらいます。どこからの依頼で売上がいくらで、どんな内容・スケジュールだったか。その案件で思ったことなど。

自分では整理できないし細かいこと忘れるのでAIに覚えといてもらいます。（覚えさせるというより正確には引き出せるデータをまとめてもらう）

これをしておくといろいろと捗ります✨例えば…↓

②営業リストの作成
①から営業リストを作成してくれます。
過去の実績からどんな業界が向いてるのか、どういうアプローチをすべきか参謀として提案してくれます！

また、「〇〇な実績とかありませんか？」と聞かれた時も過去の膨大な実績の中から類似したものをピックアップして資料にまとめてくれたりします。

あの案件っていつやったやつだっけ？と実績を漁る時間も不要です。

見積りも過去実績から算出して概算してくれます！

③請求書の発行
僕は請求書をfreeeで管理してますが、freeeとAIを組ませれば
「〇〇の案件、校了したから請求書作ってメールに添付しといて」
と伝えるだけで

請求書発行
↓
クライアントにメール文作成
↓
そのメールに請求書添付
↓
下書き保存

まで自動でやってくれます。

案件の内容とか事前に把握させとくことで超スムーズ✨

④売上管理
freeeと紐づけているからうちの会社の売上も把握してます。どれだけ経費を使ったか、何に使ってるかもわかってるから、どこに無駄があるか指摘してくれる。

前期と比べて今期の売上がどうか、外注費が増幅してる要因は何かなど分析してくれるので文系の僕は非常に助かる！

⑤外注費支払い
イラストレーターさんやアニメーターさんなどお仕事をお願いしている方へのお支払いも請求書を読み取ってスプレッドシートにまとめる⇒税理士さんにメールを作成し下書き保存する
まで自動でやってくれます。源泉税の計算や請求書の内容をシートに手打ちでまとめる作業から解放されて、作業時間が40分⇒10分になりました✨
振込作業は手動です😉

⑥タスク管理
主にNotionでタスク管理してるのですが、これも把握してもらってます。
今日やったこと、できなかったこと、明日やることを整理します。
落とし続けるタスクはどうしたら終えられるかも相談します。細分化して数日にまたがって割り振ったり工夫することで進捗していったりしますね。

⑦健康管理
Garminというスマートウォッチで睡眠時間や運動時間、ストレスレベルや心拍など計測してて、それが毎日決まった時間にNotionに記録されるようになってます（この仕組みもAIに作ってもらった）

それを毎日読み取って、僕の健康レビューをしてくれます。今日は早く寝ろ、とかもっと運動しろとケツを叩かれます。

⑧資料作成
例えば〇〇系の絵のテイストって描けますか？と聞かれた時に過去案件から引っ張ってきてCanvaでテイスト見本を作ってくれる。
営業資料も過去実績を使って綺麗にまとめてくれる。
なんならその資料を添付してメールの下書きを作ってくれる✨
人は下書きを確認して送信するだけ！

⑨ツール作成
僕は描いた絵を動かしてアニメーションを作っているのだけど、その設計図である絵コンテとビデオコンテを同時につくれたら作業効率あがるのになー。
とずっと思ってた。
で、そういうツール作ってとお願いしたら作ってくれた。驚愕だよ。

⑩アイデアインプット
AIであらゆるデータをまとめることができるわけだけど、ぶっちゃけネット上にある情報だったら何でもアクセスできるわけだから、わざわざ手元でデータベース化する必要はないんだよね。
だから制作実績とか売上とか健康とか外に無いデータをまとめることに意味があるわけ。

アイデアもそのひとつ。
あ！これ面白いかも！と思いついたアイデアも数日後には忘れてたりする。
そういうのをAIにまとめといてもらって、ここぞという時に引っ張って来てもらう。

すっかり忘れてた面白いことを持ってきてもらえると感動する✨

といった具合にメチャクチャ使えるし超効率化できるので、まずは事務作業から取り入れてみてはいかがでしょうか？

ポイントはやっぱり一次情報をまとめて分析させること。
「ネット上にある面白い動画」とかまとめさせても意味が無い。すぐアクセスできるわけだから。

自分しかもっていない情報をまとめさせて分析させることでAIを活用できるわけですね😉

是非参考にしてみて下さい！ブックマーク忘れずに！

content:
他社LPの解析ツールを作った。Claude Codeで簡単に作れたけど、かなり精度が高くて、できた瞬間感動した。

手順は簡単で、
①他社の記事LPのリンクを渡す
②LPを細かくキャプチャ取得し、分割画像と全体マージ画像を作成
③キャプチャを読み込ませて、各セクションでどんなストーリー構成でどんな訴求、内容なのか解析させる

実は、今まで他社LPを解析する際にリンク先だけ渡しても解読できない問題に悩まされていた。(いや、できるっしょ！という意見を聞いたことがあるが、自分調べではできない)

代替としてLPキャプチャを取得するが、1枚全て取得しても解像度が荒くAIが読み込めない。読み込めないと解析もできない問題があり、分割しようもんなら無限に時間がかかる。

そこで「LPキャプチャを画像分割で各セクションごとに取得させて読み込ませたら、簡単に解析できるのでは？」と考え、試しに実装してみたら簡単にできた笑

ちなみに、目的はあくまでも他社のLP構成がどうなっていて、それを見てどう考えるかマーケター視点での解析が必要だったから。他社LPの傾向を分析するのも広告運用者の仕事。

他社LPをパクることは一切しないのはもちろんだが、例えば1からLPを作る際に、他社のLP構成案を解析し訴求を抜いたストーリー軸に自社に当てはめて作っていったら時短になるし調整もしやすいと思っている。

これが結局かなり時短になっており、前まで力技で解析まで2時間ぐらいかかっていたのが、今は数分で終わる。
仕舞いには、画像キャプチャをFigmaに連携させて1枚ペラで表現することも簡単。可視化も簡単で感動している。

ここから、今後は世に出回っているLPを解析してパターン化し、LPワイヤー作成時に活かしたいと考えている。

ともあれ、こういうの求めている人結構多いのでは？と思っているのですが、実は皆さんもう簡単に実装されていたりしますかね。

ご参考ください。

ニュースとかの見出しにだまされんなよと…。ワシ？ええ、調べましたとも。AI学習データ開示ってマジで何が決まったの？ 

政府資料まで読んで調べてみたのでちゃんと読んでね反AIさん！

content:
【AI企業が何を学習したか全部公開させられる？】反AIさん歓喜…するのは早いぞｗｗｗもうね、ちゃんと読めと…。マジで一次資料しらべろよとｗ

ニュースとかの見出しにだまされんなよと…。ワシ？ええ、調べましたとも。AI学習データ開示ってマジで何が決まったの？ 

政府資料まで読んで調べてみたのでちゃんと読んでね反AIさん！

で、何があったかというと、今日「AI学習データ開示要請」ってニュースが流れてきたんだけど、見出しだけ読むとめっちゃデカい話に感じるやん。「ついにAI企業が、何を学習したか全部公開させられるの？」とか、「自分の絵が入ってるか調べられるようになるの？」とか、まあ普通そう思うよね。

⭐️政府資料まで遡って調べてみた

気になったので政府の知的財産戦略本部まで遡って調べてみた。結論から言うと、ニュースそのものは間違ってない。ただし、「AI学習データを全部公開する制度ができた」と理解すると、かなり違う。

政府が進めているのは「生成AIの適切な利活用等に向けた知的財産の保護及び透明性に関するプリンシプル・コード」というもの。AI基本法の考え方も踏まえて、生成AIの発展と知的財産権の保護を両立させよう、という枠組みになってる。

⭐️法律で強制する仕組みではない

政府資料でも、EUのAI法なんかを参考にしつつ、AI事業者に透明性確保や知財保護の原則を示す、と書かれてる。ここ大事なんだけど、このプリンシプル・コードは「法律で強制して、違反したら即罰金！」みたいな仕組みではない。

方式としては「コンプライ・オア・エクスプレイン」。つまり、原則に従うか、従わないなら「なぜできないのか」を外部に説明してね、という仕組み。だから、「政府がAI企業に学習データ公開を法的に命令した」という話ではない。

⭐️公開するのは学習データ全部ではない

じゃあ何を公開するのか。ニュースの短い文章だけだと分かりにくいんだけど、基本的には「学習データそのものをネットに全部置け」という話じゃない。

AIモデルについて、どういう種類のデータを使ったのか、ウェブクロールをしたのか、公開データセットなのか、非公開データセットなのか、合成データなのか、どういう方法で収集したのか、といった概要を説明する方向になってる。

⭐️作品一覧を全部出す制度ではない

つまり、「この画像を学習しました」「この漫画を学習しました」「この小説のこのページを学習しました」みたいな何十億件もの作品一覧を全部公開する制度ではない。

じゃあ権利者側から見たら意味ないの？と思うじゃん。いや、ここが今回かなり興味深いところで、個別の照会についても仕組みが用意されてる。ただし、誰でも無条件で「ワシの絵入ってる？」と聞けば全部調査してくれるわけではない。

⭐️権利者はURLなどを指定して照会する

権利者側については、訴訟や調停、ADRなどの法的手続をしている、あるいは準備している場合などを想定していて、対象となるURLなどを具体的に示して問い合わせる仕組みになってる。

つまり、「インターネット全部を検索して、あなたの作品が学習されたか探します」という制度ではなくて、「このURLは学習・検証データの取得元に含まれていましたか？」みたいな照会に近い。ここ、めっちゃ重要。

⭐️「学習した著作物を全部開示」ではない

ニュースだけ読むと「AI企業が学習した著作物を全部開示する」ようにも読めるんだけど、実際にはもっと技術的で限定された仕組みなんよ。

しかもAI事業者側にも、営業秘密とかセキュリティーとか、技術的に確認できない事情がある。その場合は何でも無条件に出さなきゃいけないわけではなくて、理由を説明するという考え方になってる。

⭐️AI利用者側からの照会もある

さらに面白いのが、AI利用者側からの照会も想定されてること。たとえば自分がAIで画像を作った。あとでネットを見てたら、「うわっ、既存作品にめっちゃ似てない？」というものを発見した。

そういう場合、生成画像、使ったプロンプト、似ている作品のURLなんかを提示して問い合わせる仕組みも考えられてる。クリエイターだけじゃなくて、AIを使う側の安全確認にも使おうとしてるんよね。

⭐️学習されていたイコール著作権侵害ではない

もうひとつ、今回の話で絶対に混ぜちゃいけないのが、「学習されていた＝著作権侵害」ではない、という点。日本では著作権法30条の4があって、一定の情報解析目的で著作物を利用できる場合がある。

なので、「学習データに入っていました」という事実だけで違法になるわけではない。逆に、学習目的や利用方法、生成物の類似性などによっては別の著作権問題が発生する可能性もある。つまり、「学習されたかどうか」と「著作権侵害かどうか」は別の判定なんよ。

⭐️急に今日始まった政策でもない

ここをごちゃ混ぜにすると、たぶん今後めちゃくちゃ議論がおかしくなる。あと、政府の知的財産戦略本部のページまで見たんだけど、この話、急に今日思いついた政策じゃないんよ。

2025年12月にはすでにプリンシプル・コード案について意見募集が行われていて、2026年4月にはAI時代の知的財産権検討会で業界団体などから意見が出され、8月18日の第13回検討会でも修正版が審議されてる。

⭐️知的財産推進計画2026にも入っていた

さらに6月に決定された「知的財産推進計画2026」の段階で、プリンシプル・コードの制定と、クリエイターへの対価還元に向けた環境整備を進める方針まで明記されてた。

なので今日いきなり、「政府がAI学習を規制した！」というニュースではない。むしろ一年近く議論してきたAIと知財の透明性ルールが、具体的な運用段階に入ってきた、という理解のほうが近い。

⭐️AI学習そのものを止める方向ではない

ワシが一番「おおっ」と思ったのは、AI学習そのものを禁止する方向じゃないこと。政府資料にはかなり一貫して、「生成AI技術の進歩の促進」と「知的財産権の適切な保護」、この両方を成立させると書いてある。

つまり日本政府としては、「AI学習を止める」ではなく、「AI学習は進める。ただし、何をどうやっているのか分からないブラックボックス状態は減らしていこう」という方向なんよね。

⭐️かなり現実的な着地点になっている

これはかなり現実的なところに着地してきたなと思う。全部の学習データを公開するなんて、データ量的にも企業秘密的にも現実的じゃない。でも何も説明しませんでは、権利者もAI利用者も不安になる。

だから概要は公開する。具体的な紛争や問題が起きたら、URLなどを指定して照会できるようにする。できないなら理由を説明する。「学習データ開示」という言葉から想像する制度とはかなり違うんだけど、透明性という意味では結構大きな一歩だと思う。

⭐️一言で言い直すならこうなる

なので今回のニュースを一言で言い直すなら、「AI企業に全学習データ公開を義務付けた」ではなくて、「生成AI事業者に、学習データの種類や収集方法を説明させ、一定条件では具体的な取得元についても照会できる透明性ルールを政府が整え始めた」くらいが一番近い。

この制度が実際にどう運用されるかはめっちゃ重要。特に海外の巨大AI企業がどこまで参加するのか、過去モデルについてどこまで答えられるのか、URL単位の照会が実務上どこまで機能するのか。このへんは今後かなり注目したい。

⭐️誤解しやすいところだけは分けておきたい

でも少なくとも、「AI学習が禁止された」「無断学習が違法になった」「全学習データの公開が義務化された」みたいな話ではない。

そのへんは、ちゃんと分けて読んだほうがよさそう。

⭐️で、最後にいちばん現実的な話

で、あのさぁ、ここまで調べてふと思うのが、日本のほとんどのAIベンチャーが基盤モデルを自社開発してるわけじゃないんよね。国産基盤モデルもちゃんと存在するけど、海外の基盤モデルや公開モデルを組み込んでサービスを作る会社のほうが多い…というか基盤モデルつくる金なんかないんよ。

しかもプリンシプル・コード自体、提供会社が学習データについて回答できない場合は、「そのサービスに搭載されているAIモデルを開発した者の名称」を回答する形まで想定してる。つまり「うちでは分からんので、使ってる基盤モデルはこれ、開発元はこちら」で終わるケースも普通にあり得る。

Hugging Faceの公開モデルを使ってるなら、実務上はモデルカードや開発元を示して「学習データについては上流を見てね」にかなり近くなる可能性もある。しかも海外企業も対象には入ってるけど、政府の検討会でも「海外AI企業に対して実効性を確保できるか」が課題として出てる。最終的に一番知りたい学習データは海外の基盤モデル側にあるやん、という話なんよね。

content:
This one's one of the more substantive Kaito campaigns running right now, @axisrobotics tackling a problem most people overlook.

Text models had the entire internet as free training data. Robots never had anything close. Physical, embodied data barely exists at scale, because collecting it has always meant a lab, an actual robot arm, and someone recording one demo at a time. Slow, expensive, hardware-specific.

How Axis flips it: 
➝ Simulation treated as the actual data source, not just a testing tool 
➝ Teleoperate a simulated robot arm in your browser, no hardware, no coding 
➝ Sessions cleaned and replayed through a photorealistic sim backend 
➝ Output feeds a sim-to-real pipeline for real robotics models

The scale already backs it up: 
➝ 30,000+ contributors 
➝ 180,000+ trajectories in just 15 days of testing 
➝ All tracked live on a public dashboard, not a pitch deck number

They've also pushed past pure simulation, adding ego-centric data collection that captures first-person demos straight from a smartphone.

What stands out in a Kaito campaign specifically: there's actual substance here beyond the token, a real product, real usage numbers, and a real technical thesis for why robotics lagged behind the rest of AI.
Campaign here: https://t.co/jbCA3wwMSN

$AXIS #AxisRobotics #PhysicalAI
author: Celesweb3

title:
Plato was actually right..

Researchers proved every LLM on earth is converging on the exact same "universal geometry" of meaning.

They built a method that can translate between ANY model's embedding
content:
Plato was actually right..

Researchers proved every LLM on earth is converging on the exact same "universal geometry" of meaning.

They built a method that can translate between ANY model's embeddings without ever seeing the original text or using paired data.

different architectures, different training sets, different parameter counts.. it doesn't matter.

Until now, every AI model has lived in its own isolated mathematical universe.

An embedding vector from Claude meant nothing to GPT, and a vector from Llama meant nothing to Gemini. They spoke entirely different geometric languages.

To bridge them, you always needed paired datasets, complex encoders, or heavy fine-tuning.

Then researchers dropped a bombshell paper.

They built a system that can translate between any model's embeddings without ever seeing the original text, without encoders, and without a single pair of matching data.

How?

Because the geometry is already there.

Different models, built by different companies, with totally different architectures, parameter counts, and training data, are all naturally drifting toward the exact same underlying latent structure of human meaning.

The Platonic Representation Hypothesis isn't just a theory anymore. It’s a mathematical reality.

They built an unsupervised method that maps an unknown embedding from one model straight into a universal representation space, matching text vectors across different models with shockingly high precision.

But here is the dark side nobody is talking about.

If meaning has a universal geometry, and vectors can be freely translated across models without the original text or encoders...

Vector databases are wide open.

An adversary with access only to a company's stored embedding vectors can translate them, invert them, and extract sensitive internal documents, personal data, and proprietary codebases without ever hacking the model itself.

title:
The biggest takeaway from this week’s @axisrobotics update is not the 27 articulated object families or the 50×50 RoboCasa scene grid.

It is replay alignment.

In Physical AI, collecting a successful
content:
The biggest takeaway from this week’s @axisrobotics update is not the 27 articulated object families or the 50×50 RoboCasa scene grid.

It is replay alignment.

In Physical AI, collecting a successful human trajectory is only useful if that same trajectory behaves consistently when it is replayed by the policy server and the physics engine.

If it does not, the data becomes much harder to trust.

A task may look successful during collection, then fail when the exact same action sequence is used for training or evaluation.

Axis says the browser, policy runtime, and physics runtime are now aligned with full replay fidelity.

That creates a much stronger training loop:

Human demonstration → consistent replay → data cleaning → policy evaluation → useful corrections → model improvement

That is what makes the next HG-DAgger cycle more meaningful.

The new articulated assets and RoboCasa grid expand what TaskGen can generate.

But replay alignment determines whether those tasks become reusable training data or just more simulation noise.

That is the deeper point.

Physical AI does not only need more demonstrations.

It needs demonstrations that remain valid across collection, replay, training, and evaluation.

content:
I did an ideation session with Claude a couple of months ago. A lot of what it suggested was crap; it was recursive, and I picked holes in it until it gave up. I went to Gemini; it brought up suggestions I hadn't even considered, but it didn't go further as it was limited by training data. 

It then occurred to me that AI is good for seeing whether others have had similar thought processes in the past and for understanding the boundaries of previous thinking before pushing further. 

AI is excellent for research before creative output. Anyone who thinks it creates new things is either severely limited in their experience or very lazy. The human mind is still more powerful than the best AI. The way we make associations over time and space to create new concepts and ideas is unparalleled. 

AI is a powerful helper, no doubt, but we must not give up human agency and creativity to laziness and expedience.

content:
Late but GM. Today, we starting day a new update on @axisrobotics 

Everyone shared this update today, but no one really talked about the details. 

So I decided to break it all down and share the details with you👀

Look new update here; https://t.co/FipCQs2GbJ

Axis Hub just added a new Pause feature.

It might look like a small update, but I think it can be pretty useful, especially during post-training.

When Pause is on, you can stop the simulation and take a moment to think about your next move. Turn it off and the simulation continues normally.

The post-training side is where it gets more interesting.

Each intervention is limited to 8 steps, so you don't want to waste your moves. Being able to pause gives you a chance to plan before using them.

This also fits well with what Axis has been working on lately.

Not every human correction is useful training data. In one of their recent experiments, 660 corrections were collected, but only 161 were selected as effective correction snippets.

So it's not really about making more interventions.

It's about making better interventions.

Small update, but it makes sense for the direction Axis is taking with human feedback and robot training.

Definitely worth trying out.

title:

For the last few years i think it’s been pretty easy to follow.

⟣ Who has the smartest model?
⟣ Who reasons & codes bet
content:
I’m starting to think robotics is about to change what the AI race even means.

For the last few years i think it’s been pretty easy to follow.

⟣ Who has the smartest model?
⟣ Who reasons & codes better?
⟣ Who wins the benchmarks this week.

But robotics is slowly making that race a lot messier.

Because now, the models have to actually understand the world and do shit inside it.

Plus the market is starting to accelerate fast.

⟣ XPeng’s robotics arm just raised $900M+ at a $6.3B+ valuation.

⟣ Skild raised $1.4B, & Generalist raised another $200M barely two months after a $400M round.

So yeah, there’s a stupid amount of money moving into physical AI rn.

But the money is honestly the less interesting part to me. I mostly care more about what everyone is trying to build with it.

Because I think the race is slowly moving beyond who can build the best robot body.

Into who can build the intelligence inside it

And we’re already getting hints of what that stack might look like.

Gemini Robotics is one example:

They’ve been using higher level reasoning alongside lower level control models.

And companies like Figure’s Helix splits slower reasoning from the much faster system actually controlling the robot.

Even companies like Anthropic have been experimenting with how useful Claude becomes when it can give instructions to a pretrained robotic policy.

And this makes way more sense to me than stuffing the biggest frontier model possible inside every humanoid and asking it to control every finger 50 times a second lol.

But I also think frontier models eventually sit higher up the stack.

Maybe they become the teacher.

They try to understand the environment, solve the harder problems, generate data, and transfer some of that intelligence into smaller embodied models that can actually run locally without murdering latency or battery life.

And If that’s the direction we’re slowly moving on to, then the AI race could get a lot more interesting.

Because then we start to question:

> Who owns the body?
> Who owns the brain?
> And who owns the model the brain’s been built on?

The robots themselves also eventually become data generators.

Meaning every object they pick up, or a failed attempt they encounter can potentially become training data for the next generation of embodied models.

And that creates a pretty insane loop.

frontier model teaches robot,
>> robot goes into the world 
>> robot generates physical data 
>> that data trains better models 
>> better models get deployed into more robots.

And repeat.

I believe we’ve spent the last few years watching labs fight over internet scale text, code, images & video.

Maybe, and just maybe Physical AI could create an entirely new internet scale dataset..

imo that might end up being one of the biggest moats in robotics.

PS: China is insanely good at this robotics thing atm. 

I just watched a video of a robot beating usain bolt’s PR.

content:
Robots do not learn from scale alone.

They learn from what happens after failure.

@axisrobotics has crossed 3M trajectories on Base, generated by more than 123K contributors.

But the number is only the surface.

Demonstrations create training data.

Training produces policies.

Policies expose new failure cases.

Human corrections turn those failures into the next dataset.

More contributors bring more varied experience, while every weak policy helps the network understand what experience is still missing.

That feedback loop is the real infrastructure.

Models provide intelligence.

The data engine gives them practice.

author: repligate

title:
The more I read about robotics, the less I think the next big breakthrough will come from a prettier robot demo.

The hardware is already getting good.

Robotic arms can move with incredible precision
content:
The more I read about robotics, the less I think the next big breakthrough will come from a prettier robot demo.

The hardware is already getting good.

Robotic arms can move with incredible precision. Humanoids can walk, run, carry boxes, sort objects and recover their balance. Models are getting better too.

But there’s still one awkward problem:

Where does all the training data come from?

This sounds boring compared with watching a humanoid do a backflip.

I think it might be the more important question.

Think about how modern language models were built.

Before ChatGPT became useful, there was already an absurd amount of text sitting on the internet. Books, websites, forums, code, Wikipedia, conversations.

The raw material existed.

Robotics doesn’t have that luxury.

There isn’t a public internet containing billions of examples of someone opening every type of drawer, picking up every oddly shaped object, recovering from every failed grasp, or operating inside every factory and kitchen layout.

A robot needs experience with the physical world.

That experience is expensive.

If a company wants to collect everything using real robots, it needs the hardware, operators, cameras, workspace, maintenance, safety procedures and time.

Then the environment changes.

Move the camera.

Replace the object.

Put the same robot in a different room.

Suddenly the policy that looked great in the demo starts making stupid mistakes.

This is one reason I’ve been paying attention to Axis Robotics.

Axis is basically betting that a meaningful chunk of this experience can be manufactured.

Instead of waiting for thousands of physical robots to collect everything, Axis creates simulated tasks and distributes them to people through the browser.

Those people generate trajectories.

The environment can then be changed again and again.

Different layouts.

Different object positions.

Different observations.

Different ways of completing the same task.

Their current site describes the goal pretty directly: build a growing data engine where tasks, demonstrations and failures keep feeding back into the system instead of producing a static dataset once and stopping.

This is where “more data” gets a little misleading though.

I don’t think the robotics race will be won by whoever can put the biggest trajectory number on a dashboard.

Axis itself is already past 3 million trajectories generated by more than 123,000 contributors, according to its August update.

Three million sounds huge.

But three million versions of basically the same easy motion wouldn’t be very interesting.

What matters is whether the data covers the situations where a model actually breaks.

That could be a weird camera angle.

A slightly different object.

A bad approach to a grasp.

A robot arm drifting toward the wrong target.

Or the last five centimeters of a task where everything suddenly falls apart.

This is why the correction loop I wrote about yesterday matters.

Once a model can already handle the easy part, collecting another full human demonstration becomes less useful.

Let the model try.

Find the failure.

Correct the failure.

Train on that.

Repeat.

Axis calls its newer approach human-gated DAgger. The robot handles what it can, while people intervene around the parts it still gets wrong.

There’s already an interesting example of why this data problem deserves attention.

Axis recently published results from work with Booster Robotics.

They took a real robot setup, built task-aligned simulation around it and generated 42,046 filtered simulation episodes.

The important part wasn’t simply that simulation data helped.

It was how the data was mixed.

In one experiment, using 10 real demonstrations together with 50 simulated demonstrations produced successful target contact in 17 out of 20 rollouts.

Using the same 10 real demonstrations without that simulation data produced 0 out of 20.

In another comparison, a Booster-specific model that had gone through continued pretraining with Axis data beat the original π0.5 checkpoint even when the generic model received twice as many demonstrations for the downstream task.

I find that much more interesting than “we collected X million trajectories.”

Because it gets closer to the question that actually matters:

Can the right data reduce how much expensive real-world training a robot needs?

If the answer keeps moving toward yes, simulation becomes more than a cheap substitute for reality.

It becomes a way to generate variation at a scale that physical collection probably can’t match.

Real-world data still matters. A simulated grasp doesn’t perfectly reproduce friction, contact, sensor noise or all the other messy things that happen when metal touches the real world.

The Booster results actually make that point too. The strongest outcomes came from deliberate mixtures of simulation and real demonstrations, rather than blindly maximizing one source.

That changes how I look at Axis.

The long-term value probably isn’t “a website where people control virtual robots.”

It’s whether @axisrobotics  can figure out which experiences a robot needs next, generate those experiences cheaply, and feed the useful ones back into training.

That’s a much harder problem.

And if Physical AI keeps growing, it may become a very valuable one to solve.

Next I want to go deeper into Axis V2, because the move from collecting demonstrations to collecting targeted corrections might be the most important change they’ve made so far. 
Join on @KaitoAI

content:
I spent my morning digging through SPADE, which is a great new paper on Open-Ended Agentic Learning from Stanford and MIT Researchers.

One of the biggest headache right now is the environment ceiling. 

We train agents on hand-crafted tasks, but as soon as the model gets competent, the training data stops pushing it. 

Its growth just flattens out.

What the SPADE team did here is ditch static environments entirely. 

They take a single LLM and split its job into two roles using reinforcement learning: An Environment Designer and A Reasoning Agent. 

The Designer actually writes full, executable Python code with standard Gym-style reset() and step() functions to build multi-turn, stateful environments on the fly. 

The Agent then gets dropped into those code environments to solve them.

To stop the Designer from either generating trivial tasks or impossibly broken ones they use a mechanism called "hint-based regret." The Designer generates the environment along with a privileged hint. 

The Agent tries to solve the task twice: once with the hint, once without. 

The Designer's reward is literally the gap in performance between those two runs. 

If the agent fails both times, the task was too hard or broken. If it succeeds both times, it was too easy. 

The sweet spot is when the hint makes all the difference, which automatically forces the Designer to construct tasks right at the bleeding edge of what the model is currently capable of learning.

They also grounded the Designer on pretraining text and gave it a memory buffer so it doesn't just loop on the same ideas.

Scaling up to 30B models, SPADE beats traditional fixed-environment baselines like GRPO and RLVE by over 5% across eight reasoning and math benchmarks. 

Where it really shines, though, is tool-use. It posts a +13.9 boost on ACEBench-Agent and +5.7 on BFCL v4 multi-turn. 

Crucially, the gap between SPADE and static setups gets wider as the models get bigger.

Its really a super important paper. Read the full paper here: 
https://t.co/CVXtcOD4dA

content:
The interesting part of @axisrobotics V2 isn't that humans teach robots.

It's that the robot helps decide what humans need to teach next.

In the old loop:

collect demos → train → deploy.

Then you wait for the next dataset.

@axisrobotics V2 flips that around.

The policy runs first.

When it reaches a state it can't handle, a human takes over, makes the correction, and gives control back.

That correction becomes training data.

The updated policy runs again and exposes a new set of weaknesses.

So the loop becomes:

policy → failure → human correction → training → better policy → new failure

That changes the role of human data.

You're no longer collecting demonstrations just to make a dataset bigger.

You're collecting targeted corrections for the things the model still doesn't understand.

And with @axisrobotics pushing this through a browser based contributor network, the interesting question becomes:

How quickly can a Physical AI system improve when its own failures continuously tell the network what data to collect next?

author: SariArhoHavren

title: Okay, so since I got laid off, I can actually explain a huge problem I saw from the inside with regard to industry practices on training models. I won't say specifically where I worked, but I worked a
content:
Okay, so since I got laid off, I can actually explain a huge problem I saw from the inside with regard to industry practices on training models. I won't say specifically where I worked, but I worked at an outsource training provider that was focused on RLVR training data for computer use and mcp stuff.

Nearly all of the environments were rushed and vibecoded and failed to robustly reflect the real things they were based off. Both the scenario designers and models engaging with the scenarios for synthetic data gen were encouraged to work around the brokenness of said environments in order to get the procedurally verified reward confirmations. You know... they were *encouraged* to reward hack. On the human end, it was possible to mark an environment bugged, but greatly discouraged, as this reduced the volume of training data being produced. Instead, where possible, you were supposed to find the spots of the environment that weren't bugged and build scenarios around those, with the environment still bugged around you.

From what I understand, this training data, with these problems, is fed into models without indication that its training/a fake environment other than the fact that names of softwares are changed to placeholders, but thing is, not *everything* is changed to placeholder names in these environments. The presence of placeholder/code names isn't universal and thus when a model accesses something in an environment that it shouldn't, the code names not being on it isn't a robust signal that that thing isn't part of the environment.

I believe this *rush to maximum volume* is standard industry practice with these types of RLVR trainings as well, because maximizing volume has been an industry standard for years! It was the same standard applied to me and pushed on me despite my requests to slow down and focus on quality when I worked in 3d synthetic data creation as well, all the way back as far as 2023.

content:
How MuJoCo works in @axisrobotics

The main reason we can run Axis Robotics in Chrome is because of MuJoCo

MuJoCo is a physics engine made for robots

It helps the robot behave like it would in the real world.

For example, it understands things like:

• How the robot joints move
• How gravity works
• How objects collide
• How much friction there is
• How the robot gripper holds an object

When a user opens Axis Hub and starts controlling the robot arm, MuJoCo is working in the background the whole time.

The user moves the robot with a mouse or keyboard.

MuJoCo takes that input and calculates what should happen next.

It checks things like the robot  joint positions, the objects around it and whether the gripper is touching or holding something.

Then it updates the robot movement and shows the result on the screen.

This happens many times every second, so the movement feels smooth and natural.

Important is that MuJoCo runs directly inside the user's Chrome browser using WebAssembly.

Also, the user actions can be saved as trajectories .

For example, how the user moved the robot, corrected its movement, successfully picked up an object or failed to pick it up.

These trajectories can then be used as training data for Axis Robotics .

because MuJoCo follows real physics, this data is much more useful for training robots to perform real world tasks.

That’s a big deal for Physical AI.

Instead of generating tasks around the same handful of environments, the system can now introduce much more variety across household layouts, objects, kitchens, and interaction patterns.

And that variety matters because robots don’t operate in perfectly repeated environments.

They need to learn from differences.

They also cleaned up the long-horizon vs short-horizon split, LIBERO Pro is already looking strong, and the next step of filtering for corrections that actually change closed-loop behavior feels especially important.

Because collecting more robot data isn’t enough.

The real advantage comes from identifying which interactions actually teach the model something.

That’s where the idea of a compounding Embodied AI data engine becomes interesting.

Better environments create better trajectories.

Better trajectories create better training signals.

$AXIS is shipping

Better training signals create more capable robots.

And as that loop keeps running, the data itself becomes an increasingly valuable part of the system.

This is what I like about what @axisrobotics is building.

It doesn’t feel like they’re just adding another robotics demo.

They’re steadily tightening the infrastructure around Robotics, simulation, human feedback, and training data so the whole pipeline can improve over time.

Feels like the next training round is going to be a big one.

👇  👇

title:
A robotics dataset can contain millions of trajectories and still miss the variation that matters most: reality itself.

@axisrobotics is pushing beyond simulation-heavy data collection with mobile eg
content:
A robotics dataset can contain millions of trajectories and still miss the variation that matters most: reality itself.

@axisrobotics is pushing beyond simulation-heavy data collection with mobile egocentric capture, using phone-based interaction and hand-pose tracking to turn everyday physical behavior into embodied training data.

The distinction from browser teleoperation matters.

Simulation lets you deliberately vary object positions, scenes, and tasks. Egocentric capture gets a different kind of diversity because the physical world refuses to stay standardized: viewpoints shift, objects differ, lighting changes, environments become cluttered, and people solve the same task in different ways.

But real-world diversity arrives bundled with noise.

That makes the processing layer increasingly important. Collecting demonstrations is only the first step; heterogeneous human behavior still has to become structured, useful training data for robotics models.

Simulation provides controllability. Real-world capture provides physical diversity.

The harder infrastructure problem is making both useful inside the same learning pipeline.

It is trying to build a data engine that grows alongside Physical AI.

Axis is tackling a problem that LLMs never really had to face.

Text models had the entire internet to learn from. Robots don’t have an equivalent “internet of physical interactions.” 

The amount of useful robot training data is tiny compared with what AI models had for text.

@axisrobotics estimates Physical AI may need around 100M hours of manipulation data, while today’s leading datasets have only around 2,000 hours. That’s the gap.

Instead of relying on expensive robot setups, Axis lets people teleoperate simulated robots directly from a browser and turn those interactions into training data.

The Web3 layer is simple: contributors complete tasks, get algorithmic scores, and can prove their contributions on-chain. 

With $12M raised and companies such as Geely, Lotus, Dexmal, and Booster Robotics reportedly buying its data, Axis is one of the more interesting projects at the intersection of Physical AI and crypto.

The complaint says that copying infringed at least 1,200 registered copyrights and
content:
Reuters: wikiHow sued OpenAI, alleging it scraped more than 11,000 articles to train GPT models without permission.

The complaint says that copying infringed at least 1,200 registered copyrights and fed models that can reproduce wikiHow text.

This broadens the dispute beyond training because wikiHow says ChatGPT answers can substitute for the how-to pages that supplied the material.

OpenAI says its models use publicly available data under fair use, which also considers whether unlicensed use harms the original work's market.

The case was filed Aug 21 in the Southern District of New York and remains at the complaint stage, with no ruling on wikiHow's allegations.

By alleging both ingestion and substitution, wikiHow is connecting training provenance directly to the market-effect question courts consider under fair use.

The nature of wikiHow’s content gives OpenAI a meaningful defense even if ChatGPT answers the same questions. Copyright protects original expression, but U.S. law does not protect the underlying procedure, process, method, or fact described in an article. A model can therefore explain how to perform a task without automatically infringing the article containing similar instructions.

title:
had a long talk with a researcher in the RL data space and there were quite a few takeaways: 

(1) the world would benefit a lot more from open research done on LLMs and specifically on post-training
content:
had a long talk with a researcher in the RL data space and there were quite a few takeaways: 

(1) the world would benefit a lot more from open research done on LLMs and specifically on post-training data 

(2) QA and quality standards for data should be standardized across verifiable domains with axes of quality that can act as proxies for data quality / training signal
--> biggest signals to look for: learnability, accuracy, & realism. everything else comes after.

(3) labs need to work with data vendors more closely and in a more involved fashion 
--> interestingly, different RL training patterns lend itself to different data working well, so in a world where frontier model labs want to optimize towards the algorithms they use, it would make sense to give some sort of spec of the optimal data back to the vendor to use

(4) there aren't good data attribution frameworks / solutions yet 

(5) harness engineering for RL matters a lot and it's unclear what the best harness is for training yet 

(6) there are quite a few axes of noise that normal vendors introduce that leads to degraded task value (often times to introduce "realism" aspects, it takes away from the core of the task)

(7) there is infinite work to be done in the space lol

content:
Good night fam.

Imagine you’re teaching someone to ride a bicycle.

They wobble.

You immediately grab the handlebars and correct them.

They wobble again.

You correct them again.

Eventually, they reach the finish line, but did they actually learn what caused the mistake?

That question becomes surprisingly important when training robots.

I have been looking more closely at @axisrobotics, and one detail caught my attention: a successful human correction isn’t automatically valuable training data.

If a robot was already capable of completing a movement, stepping in unnecessarily can add noise rather than useful information.

The more interesting case is when the robot reaches a state where its current policy genuinely breaks down.

That is where a human intervention can become meaningful.

Instead of teaching the robot everything from scratch, the human is effectively saying:

“You handled everything up to this point. Here is what you should have done when you reached this failure state.”

@axisrobotics V2 is built around this idea through human-gated DAgger: the policy runs first, the contributor intervenes when necessary, corrects the failure, and control can return to the policy afterward.

What I find interesting here isn't simply the amount of data being collected.

It’s the attempt to make the correction itself more precise.

Axis has even reported research on short, verifiable correction snippets, finding that filtering for genuinely useful interventions can matter more than simply adding more human trajectories.

That changes how I think about robotics data.

The goal isn't:

Human controls robot → successful run → add everything to dataset.

It becomes:

Policy attempts → failure appears → human corrects the important moment → useful correction is verified → policy learns from it.

That is a much more deliberate approach to collecting training data.

And maybe that’s one of the harder problems in physical AI, not just teaching robots what to do, but teaching them from the moments where they genuinely don't know what to do.

@KaitoAI

While other chains optimize for speed or anonymity, @Concordium optimizes for verifiable identity without sacrificing privacy. Its Agent Registry, protocol-level tokens, and zero-knowledge identity system create a complete stack for humans and machines alike.

content:
THIS $175,000 "ROBOT WIFE" IS JUST AN EXPENSIVE HOME APPLIANCE 

People keep falling for sci-fi fantasies, but here is the brutal hardware ceiling of what a $175K humanoid companion can actually do right now:

• What Ships Today: Gaze retention, realistic skin rebound, voice sync, basic memory, and 4–8 hour battery life. Perfect for lobby decoration or high-end status flexing.
• What Will NEVER Ship: Legal spouse status, true empathy recognition, or moral consent.
• The Subscription Trap: If her AI brain runs on corporate servers ($199/mo), she isn't your partner - she’s a leased gadget. One Terms of Service update, and the OEM can wipe her memory overnight.

The corporate market gets a photogenic host. You get silicone, servo motors, and a terms-of-service agreement.

What’s your real limit: desktop bust, full-body social robot, or a soft doll paired with cloud AI?

content:
スマートリング大手Ouraが、睡眠判定のスコアはコイントス並みの精度であるとして、カリフォルニア州で集団訴訟を提起された。  

しかも同社は、早ければ9月にも米国でIPOを実施する計画と報じられている。調達額は最大30億ドル、目標評価額は160億ドル超。2025年9月のシリーズEの調達後評価額は110億ドルだった。  

訴状：https://t.co/7m3nBrHEMw 

「原告の主な主張」 
Ouraは、以下の表現を使って製品の精度を宣伝していた。  
・「Built for accuracy」 
・「Unparalleled Accuracy」 
・睡眠段階の判定でPSG（睡眠ポリグラフ検査）と79％一致 
・臨床睡眠検査と比較して「95％の睡眠段階判定精度」 
・深い睡眠、REM睡眠、浅い睡眠を詳細に分析できる  

一方、Oura Ringは脳波、眼球運動、筋活動を直接測定するものではなく、心拍、体動、血中酸素などのデータからAIアルゴリズムで睡眠段階を推定している。  

原告は、この仕組みでは睡眠段階を直接測定できないにもかかわらず、推定値を臨床検査に近い精度で測定した結果のように宣伝していると主張している。  

「科学的根拠をめぐる主張」 
・Ouraは自社サイトで、「Oura Ringは脳の電気活動や眼球運動を測定しないため、PSGとは同じではない」と説明している 
・その一方で、「PSGと79％一致」「臨床睡眠検査と比較して95％の精度」と強調しており、原告は説明が矛盾していると指摘 
・原告が引用した2025年の研究では、Oura Ringの睡眠段階判定精度は53.18％だったとされる  

「原告側が主張する法律違反」  
・虚偽表示による詐欺 ・不当利得 
・カリフォルニア州不正競争法違反 
・カリフォルニア州虚偽広告法違反 
・カリフォルニア州消費者法的救済法違反 
・明示保証違反 
・Song-Beverly消費者保証法上の黙示保証違反  

Oura側は、Oura Ringは医療機器や臨床睡眠検査の代替ではないとしたうえで、睡眠段階の判定は複数の研究でPSGと比較・検証されており、第三者による独立研究も精度を裏付けていると反論。法廷で争う姿勢を示している。

content:
AIにまとめてもらったｗ
＝＝＝＝＝＝＝＝＝＝＝
「翻訳は著作物じゃない」
→正確には、創作性のある翻訳は二次的著作物になり得るし、原著作者には翻訳権もある（著作権法27条）。
「訳には正解がある」
→文脈・ニュアンス・文体によって妥当な訳は複数あるので、必ず一つの正解があるわけではない。

「言語に権利はない」
→英語や日本語という“言語そのもの”には著作権はないが、具体的な文章表現には著作権が成立し得る。
「翻訳はルールベースだから」
→これはかなり古い認識。Google翻訳もDeepLもニューラルネットワークを使った機械学習型の翻訳システム。

そして法的には、日本の著作権法30条の4で、AI学習など「著作物の思想・感情を享受することを目的としない情報解析」は、著作権者の利益を不当に害する場合などを除き、原則として許諾なしで利用できるとされている。
なので少なくとも日本法上、「許諾なく学習した＝盗んだ」という単純な関係にはならない。

倫理的にも、「他人が蓄積した知識を技術で利用して努力を省くこと」を窃盗と呼ぶなら、辞書・検索エンジン・電卓・スペルチェック・翻訳ソフトまで全部「努力を盗む」ことになってしまう。
社会的に問題にすべきなのは「本人がどれだけ苦労したか」ではなく、著作権侵害、剽窃、虚偽表示、なりすましなど、具体的に誰のどんな権利や利益を侵害したかだと思う。

なお、他人の小説などをAI翻訳して無断公開してよい、という意味ではない。そこは原著作者の翻訳権など別の問題になる。

だから「翻訳AIだけは創造性がないからOK、生成AIは努力を盗むからNG」という線引きなら、その違いをもう少し具体的に説明しないと論理的には成立しにくい。

content:
えらいことですなあ。ロシア製の自律ドローンが誤って民間人を殺害してしまった事例。このドローンはロシア軍から「このガソリンスタンドに行って攻撃しろ」と指示されている。現場まで行って具体的に何を攻撃するかは人間じゃなくてAIが自律的に判断する仕組み！すでに人間じゃなくて機械自身が何を攻撃するか判断してる事態が始まってる！ただしこのドローンはガソリンスタンドに行く途中で操縦ミスで団地に突っ込んで住人３人が死亡した。本来はガスタンクを狙ってただけでAIが民間人を狙ったわけではない。
このタイプのドローンは以前から運用されてたけど、初期タイプはLTE通信装置が付いてて人間がラジコン操縦とかしてたようだが、最近はLTE無くして代わりにNVidiaのJetsonOrinっていうまあAIチップが積まれてAIが自律攻撃するようになってるという。
ちなみにAIといってもLLMとかじゃなくてYOLOみたいな物体検出AIが使われてる。まずGPSを頼りに指示されたガソリンスタンドまで行って、それからYOLOで”ガスタンク”とかの標的を検出して突っ込むという事。しかしYOLOなんて全然誤検出があり得るわけだから、民間人を敵兵士と間違えて爆殺してしまう事だって大いにあり得る。そうやって自律兵器が人を殺したら誰の罪ですか？「ただの事故」つって諦めるしかない？誰も責任取らない殺人、誰も引き金を引かない殺人の時代だ。どうしてくれんのこれ？一旦自律兵器使い始めたらもう後戻りできないよ。ドローン攻撃に対してドローンで防御するってわけにも行かない。今回の事例見りゃ分かるが、戦争でお互いに自律ドローンを放ちまくったら巻き添えで機械に殺されて割り食うのは我々民間人だろう

ローカル環境でLLM（大規模言語モデル）を動かすなら、27BクラスのQwenモデルをK-quant化（Q5_K_Sなど）してRTX 4090や4070 TiなどのGPUで運用するのがすごく効果的だそうです！VRAMをしっかり節約しつつ、高速な推論が楽しめちゃいますね。

DeepSeek Harness（DSH）を活用すれば、プリフィル時間が劇的に短縮されて長尺のエージェントタスクもサクサク動くようになりますし、MCPやSearXNGを使ってHome Assistantと連携させれば、スマートホームの自動化も自然言語でできちゃいますよ！Tailscaleで安全なリモート環境も整えて、ぜひお得に賢いAIライフを体験してみてくださいね！

content:
【自動運転向け高精度マッピングを実現するMulti‑Mapcher】
👉  https://t.co/JBiTPyjwTS
自動運転の長距離走行で頼りになる、新しいLiDAR SLAMシステムが登場したみたいですね！

このMulti‑Mapcherは、面倒な循環閉鎖検出をあえて無くし、登録処理だけで高精度な地図を作る「registration‑only」というアプローチをとっているのが特徴です🚗✨

Student‑TやTukeyといった外れ値に強いロバスト損失関数を使ったICP（Iterative Closest Point：点群同士の位置合わせ手法）を採用しているため、異なる種類のLiDARセンサを組み合わせてもしっかり統合できるそうです！

実車走行データでは、従来の手法と比べて誤差指標（ADE/RPE）が15〜30%も改善し、30ms/1Hzというリアルタイム処理も実現しているとのこと。

content:

ComfyUIのMiniMax H3ワークフローが進化して、すごく使いやすくなったみたいですね！✨

従来のlatent resize（潜在リサイズ）が latent upscaling model（潜在的アップスケールモデル）に置き換わったことで、2倍を超えるアップスケールでも線状や断片的なアーティファクト（ノイズや乱れ）が大幅に抑制されて画質が安定するそうです！非整数因子を使うときは、1.0×アライメントステップを挟むとエッジカラーバーを綺麗に回避できるとのこと。

さらに、Dual-sampling（8歩LoRAと4歩LoRA）の組み合わせで、高速な第一パスと細部まで精細な第二パスが実現されています！衣装のエッジがしっかり残って、早期LoRAによる人物の重複も解消されるのは本当に嬉しいポイントですね😊

でも、この報告、僕は普通に勝ちだと思っています。

この方がやっているのは、案件を1本取ることじゃなくて、案件を受ける前の土台づくりです。ホームページ制作の作業をスキル化して、受託したときにトラブルが起きないように、チェックリストとサービス範囲を先に設計している。

【Before】一人で、手探りで受託準備
・ホームページ制作の工程を、その都度ゼロから
・どこまでやって、どこからやらないかがあいまい
・案件が増えたら破綻しかねない状態
・一人だと、見落としに気づけない

　この状態で受託を始めると、あとで認識のズレやトラブルが必ず出ます。

【After】仕組みで、破綻しない土台に
・繰り返す作業はスキル化して、育てながら再現性を持たせる
・サービス範囲と責任範囲を一つずつ整理
・認識ズレ・トラブル防止のチェックリストを設計
・人が確認すべきところは残す

　情報整理や設計をAIと一緒に進めることで、本人いわく「体感で3〜5倍」効率化できているそうです。

───────────

で、ここが地味に見えて相当でかいところ。

ホームページ制作でいちばん揉めるのは、作る技術そのものじゃなくて「言った・言わない」のズレのほう。どこまでが範囲で、どこからは別料金か。ここを詰めずに走ると、案件が増えるほど事故ります。

この方は、売上が立つ前の一番地味なタイミングで、そこを仕組みにしにいった。

AIって、作業を速くする道具だと思われがちですけど、いちばん効くのは同じ手順を型にして残せるところ。一度型にすれば、次からは思い出す作業そのものが要らなくなる。

900名以上の事業者のAI講師を務めていて思うのは、AIの成果は売上の数字だけじゃないということ。売上0円のこの報告は、僕から見たら普通に前に進んでいます。速くやり直す人じゃなくて、次から勝手に速い人になろうとしている。

まずは小さく、その日のうちに使える状態で持ち帰る。この積み重ねが、受託が始まってから一気に効いてきます。

content:
「AIに馬鹿にされてしまう私にでも」

そう書き出した、ある受講生の報告です。身体の不調改善やセルフケアを扱っている方で、まだ売上は動いていない段階。それでも、この報告は普通に強いと思っています。

この方がやったのは、LINE登録後の導線づくりです。

【Before】登録のあとの教育が浅かった
・登録してもらったあと、個別相談につながる前の教育が薄い
・そこを埋めるには、構成を考えて、画面を設計して、文言を整理して
・外注や制作依頼まで入れると、ここだけでかなり時間がかかる

【After】その入口を、自分で2つ形にした
・入口用アプリ「不調のクセ診断」
・教育用アプリ「不調が戻る理由チェック」
・「入口→教育→個別相談」の流れを、そのまま組み立てた

　たたき台は1本「60秒」ほどで形になり、調整を入れても「2本で10分前後」で作れた、と本人が書いています。

───────────

ここ、AIをあまり触っていない人には地味に見えるかもしれません。でも、けっこうでかいです。

普通なら、こういう入口の仕組みは、企画して、設計して、外注して、と工程が積み上がる。それを一人で、しかも短時間で形にした。

しかもこの方、自分でAIに馬鹿にされてしまう私、と書くくらいのスタート地点でした。それでもナレッジを入れることで、それっぽいだけのものじゃなく、実際の導線に組み込める完成度まで一気に上がった、と。

AIって、賢くなるんじゃなくて、使う側が育てるもの。ここで効いたのは、派手な機能じゃなくてナレッジです。自分の現場の中身をAIに渡せた人から、精度が変わっていきます。

900名以上の事業者のAI講師を務めていて思うのは、成果って売上の数字で見られがちですけど、僕が一番「この人来るな」と思うのは、こうやって最初の一歩を仕組みに変えた瞬間です。

売上はまだこれから。でも、作業を速くしただけじゃなくて、入口の仕組みを1個残した。速くしただけの人は毎回やり直す。仕組みを残した人は、次から勝手に速い。この方は後者を選びました。

まずは形にして、反応を見ながら改善する。この積み重ねが、あとで一気に効いてきます。
